I. They were both so scared of the frenetic movements of the fat lizard in their bedroom that they decided to
spread a single mattress (the only one they had) on the living room floor. The mattress’ width enforced a kind of
intimacy that was different from what had been available on the wider bed, so much so that they soon got
talking, for the first time, about the biggest issue in their lives at that point. She told him that she really wanted
to know how he felt about her going. Knowing that, was important for her. He told her that she was going and
that was that. The important thing, he added, was whether she was sure she was going for the right reasons.
Being practical. For example, how convinced she was that the programme would lead to bigger and better job
prospects. That it would improve their finances in the medium term. She cut him short, telling him that first of
all it needed to be clear that it was he who was making things difficult by not talking about the exact reasons
why he was feeling what he was feeling. It was quite obvious that he wasn't feeling all right. Instead, she
emphasised, what he was doing at this point was to present his insecurity as her own doubt about her future,
which wasn't very helpful because of course she was a bit doubtful already and her decision to go was at some
level a leap of faith also. The living room lights were switched off and in the darkness they heard each other
breathe a couple of times before he told her that no, it was she who was making things difficult. Her decision to
go would unsettle their current lives. He asked her if she agreed and she nodded and even in the darkness he
knew that she had nodded because she was in his arms and he felt the movement on his shoulder. The most
important thing, he told her, was if she was convinced that unsettling their current lives was worth the trouble,
and that after the trouble was over their life together would be better than what they had right now. ‘Ideally, it
shouldn't be a leap of faith,” he said. That he used the word trouble for her education, she told him, told her a
lot. He tried to say something in response but she didn’t let him and silenced him by saying ‘one minute, one
minute, one minute...". How many times, she asked him then, had he been completely convinced of the outcome
of any new step that he was taking in his life? Weren't all new endeavours, she continued, leaps of faith to some
degree, and if the world went by his logic, ideally there wouldn't be anything new that anyone would ever strive
for. He snorted. She told him that there was nothing worth snorting about in what they were discussing. Of
course, there was nothing wrong with doing new things, he told her. But their situation was different. They had
to attempt to put some reason behind it. They were married. And need he also remind her what that meant. It
meant that their lives were tied. ‘The expense of your education is big,” he said, ‘and while you're sure that
you're going to finance it on your own and while that is something that I both admire and appreciate, there
shouldn't be any doubt that if the new endeavour fails, the liability of that failure will be shared by both of us,
and by our marriage. To the extent that our lives are inextricably tied, you are also deciding for me.’

II. The space traveller had been floating in the vast emptiness of space for what seemed like an eternity. The
stars that had once seemed so bright and beckoning now appeared distant and unwelcoming. The traveller's
mind began to wander, and he found himself considering the philosophical implications of Warren's thought
experiment.
Warren had proposed that if a space traveller were to be placed in a state of suspended animation for a long
period of time, during which he would be cut off from all contact with the outside world, he would no longer
exist as a person. Instead, he would be replaced by a new entity, one with identical memories and personality
but without any connection to the original person.
The space traveller found himself pondering the implications of this thought experiment as he floated in the
infinite void of space. Was he still the same person he had been when he first embarked on his journey? Had his
consciousness been transformed by the endless expanse of space and time?
As he drifted through the darkness, he began to notice a strange sensation in his body. His limbs felt heavy and
unresponsive, and he realized that he had been in a state of suspended animation for longer than he had
anticipated. The realization filled him with a sense of unease and dread, and he wondered if he had been
transformed into a new entity, one without any connection to his former self.
The traveller's mind began to race as he contemplated the implications of this realization. Was he still the same
person he had been before his journey began, or had he been transformed into something new and unknown?
Was his consciousness still intact, or had it been replaced by something else entirely?
As he grappled with these existential questions, the traveller's body began to fail him. His heart rate slowed, and
his breathing became shallow and laboured. He realized that his journey had come to an end, and that he was
about to be transformed once again, this time into something entirely different.
With a final gasp, the traveller's consciousness slipped away, leaving behind a lifeless husk floating in the
endless void of space. The implications of Warren's thought experiment suddenly became all too real, and the
traveller realized that he had been transformed into something new and unknown, something that transcended
the boundaries of space and time.

III. Compassion is a central virtue in Buddhism, and it is often seen as a panacea for all problems. The Buddha
himself was known for his boundless compassion, and he frequently taught his followers to cultivate this quality
as a means of overcoming suffering and achieving enlightenment. However, as with any virtue, compassion can
be taken too far, leading to harmful consequences for both the practitioner and those around them. One of the
dangers of excessive compassion is burnout, which can occur when caregivers or other helpers become
emotionally exhausted from constantly putting the needs of others before their own. This is particularly
common among those who work with people who are suffering, such as healthcare professionals, social
workers, and aid workers. In these contexts, the pressure to be compassionate and empathetic can be
overwhelming, leading to emotional exhaustion, depression, and other negative outcomes.
Another danger of excessive compassion is the belief that it gives one a moral authority to intervene in the lives
of others, even when their assistance is not wanted or needed. This can lead to a form of self-righteousness in
which the practitioner believes that they know what is best for others and has a duty to help them, whether they
want it or not. This can be particularly problematic when it comes to issues of cultural sensitivity and respect for

IV. One bright June morning three years ago, I was reading my Kannada newspaper as usual. It was the day the
Secondary School Leaving Certificate results had been published. While columns of roll numbers filled the
inside pages, the list of rank holders and their photographs took up almost the entire front page.
I have a great fascination for rank holders. Rank is not merely an index of one's intelligence, it also indicates the
hard work and perseverance that students have put in to reach their goal. My background—I was brought up in
a professor's family—and my own experience as a teacher have led me to believe this.
Of all the photographs in that morning's newspaper, one boy's snapshot caught my attention. I could not take my
eyes off him. He was frail and pale, but there was an endearing sparkle in his eyes. I wanted to know more
about him. I read that his name was Hanumanthappa and that he had secured the eighth rank. That was all the
information I could gather.
The next day, to my surprise, his photograph was published again, this time with an interview. With growing
interest I learned that Hanumanthappa was a coolie’s son, the oldest of five children. They belonged to a tribal
group. He was unable to study further, he said in the interview, because he lived in a village and his father, the
sole breadwinner, earned only Rs 40 a day.
I felt sorry for this bright boy. Most of us send our children to tuitions and to coaching classes, we buy them
reference books and guides, and provide the best possible facilities for them without considering the cost.
But it was different for Hanumanthappa of Rampura. He had excelled in spite of being denied some of the basic
necessities of life. While I was thinking about him with the newspaper still in my hands, I gazed at a mango tree
in my neighbour's compound. It looked its best with fresh bark, tender green leaves glistening with dewdrops
and mangoes that were about to ripen in a few days. Beyond the tree was a small potted plant that, I noticed,
had remained almost the same ever since it had been potted.
It was a calm morning. The air was cool and fresh. My thoughts were running free. The continuous whistle of
our pressure cooker broke the silence, reminding me that half an hour had passed.
Source: Wise and Otherwise, A Salute to Life by Sudha Murthy

V. Choosing the perfect gift can be a difficult task. When in doubt, flowers and fruits are always acceptable
presents. Flowers are a proud assertion of beauty and a contrast to the somewhat stern countenance of ordinary
nature. They serve as a reminder that a ray of beauty outvalues all the utilities of the world. Fruits are the flower
of commodities and can have fantastic values attached to them.
For more common gifts, necessity makes pertinences and beauty every day. It is always satisfying to supply
basic necessities like bread and water. Necessity does everything well, and in our condition of universal
dependence, it is heroic to let the petitioner be the judge of his necessity and to give all that is asked, even if it is
inconvenient. However, fantastic desires should be left to the office of punishing them by others.
A gift should properly belong to the recipient's character and be easily associated with them in thought. Tokens
of compliment and love can often be barbarous. The only true gift is a portion of oneself. It restores society to a
point where a person's biography is conveyed in their gift. It is also an index of one's merit. The poet brings his
poem, the shepherd his lamb, the farmer his corn, the miner his gem, the sailor his coral and shells, the painter
his picture, and the girl a handkerchief of her own sewing.
Buying gifts can be a lifeless business. It is fit for kings and rich men who represent kings, but not for those
who wish to give a portion of themselves. While giving gifts can be difficult, receiving them can be even harder.

and the debtor naturally wishes to give you a slap.

GENERAL KNOWLEDGE

I. India on July 13 will launch the official campaign for a non-permanent seat at the UN Security Council
According to a press note by the Ministry of External Affairs, the launch will be made by External Affairs
Minister S. Jaishankar who is currently travelling in the Gulf region and will reach New York city on July 10 for
the official ceremony that will be crucial from the point of view of India’s leadership position in the Global
South. The bid for the non-permanent seat at the UNSC comes at a time when the world is witnessing several
disruptive events such as the crisis in the Gulf following the U.S.-Israel war on Iran that has disrupted energy
and fertilizer trade with much of the world, including the Global South. The bid will also require substantial
diplomatic mobilisation by India as Tajikistan will be the other candidate for the seat meant for the Asia-Pacific
region. While India has received support from countries such as Fiji, United States, Austria and Sri Lanka, it
will have to do considerable diplomatic heavy lifting as Tajikistan has already secured the support of the OIC
bloc that consists of 57 member-states of the United Nations. That apart, both countries are members of the
SCO that will hold the next summit meeting in Kyrgyzstan, adding a special significance to the summit from
the point of view of UNSC ambitions of India and Tajikistan.

This week he is visiting Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, having visited Qatar during the weekend. He will reach
New York city for extensive consultations with India’s partners at the UN. While India has been advocating a
reform at the UNSC and also has been championing the needs of the Global South, recent trends however have
not gone according to the plans. Earlier in May, India postponed the India-Africa Forum Summit that was to be
held during May 28-31 citing the Ebola outbreak in multiple countries in Africa.

II. Last week, Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched Viksit UDAN, the next phase of the government's
flagship regional air connectivity programme, UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik), alongside the inauguration of
the new terminal building at Jodhpur airport.
Approved by the Union Cabinet in March this year, the revamped scheme aims to address the shortcomings of
the original UDAN programme while significantly expanding India's regional aviation network and
strengthening regional connectivity.
 Under the scheme, airlines bid for commercially unviable regional routes. In return for operating these routes,
they received Viability Gap Funding (VGF) from the government. Fares on a fixed number of seats were also
capped to keep air travel affordable. State governments also supported the initiative by reducing VAT on
aviation turbine fuel (ATF), providing security and fire services, and waiving several airport-related charges.
The scheme has significantly expanded India's regional aviation footprint. According to official data, UDAN
has operationalised 669 regional routes, connected 95 airports, heliports and water aerodromes, and enabled
more than 16.6 million passengers to travel under the scheme since its launch. Since its launch, commercial


flights operations reached remote destinations such as Darbhanga in Bihar, Jharsuguda in Odisha and Tezu in
Arunachal Pradesh.

Source- http://business-standard.com/industry/aviation/what-is-viksit-udan-india-s-new-push-for-regional-air-
connectivity-126070900761_1.html

III. Seeking to clarify the goals and usage implications of ethanol-blended petrol, the government has come out
with a list of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). The move comes amid backlash and concerns about the
effect of using E20 and other variants of ethanol-blended petrol on vehicles.The government has said that the
Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme is a major component of India's energy strategy, designed to
strengthen energy security, support the farming community and lower environmental impact by increasing the
use of domestically produced renewable fuel.

As a result, the regular petrol sold at fuel stations across the country now contains 20% ethanol.Fuel efficiency
continues to be the primary consideration for most buyers when choosing a vehicle. Since the nationwide
rollout of E20 fuel, many vehicle owners have complained about a decline in mileage. The issue has not only
been widely discussed on social media but has also become a frequent topic of conversation in workplaces and
social gatherings. In 2021, India required around 500 to 600 crore litres of ethanol annually to achieve 10
percent blending. As fresh investments expanded production capacity, annual ethanol availability approached
1,200 crore litres. With adequate supply in place, advancing to 20 percent blending became a logical and
responsible next step. The rise in blending tells its own story of steady, calibrated progress, not a sudden leap.

IV. The NREGA Sangharsh Morcha and the Joint Platform for Agricultural and Rural Workers’ Unions on
Wednesday announced an indefinite countrywide protest from July 1, demanding the repeal of the Viksit
Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G).
The VB-G RAM G scheme will come into force on July 1, replacing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural
Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), launched by the Congress-led UPA government in 2006. According
to the notification, the revised national average wage has now increased from ₹298.8 per day
under MGNREGA to ₹327.4 per day under VB-G RAM G, an average increase of ₹28.6 per day. It said 21
states and administrative units have been brought up to the new ₹300 interim base wage rate, while states
including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Assam will see wage increases in the range of 15
per cent to 25 per cent. Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland will see the highest percentage increase of nearly 24.5
per cent, it added.

The government said the revised wage structure has been designed to ensure that the greatest gains accrue to
states that historically had lower wage rates. It added that states with higher existing wage rates have also
received upward revisions, with Haryana having a notified wage rate of ₹409, Goa ₹406, Kerala ₹401 and
Sikkim's high-altitude gram panchayats ₹450 per day.

IV. The NREGA Sangharsh Morcha and the Joint Platform for Agricultural and Rural Workers’ Unions on
Wednesday announced an indefinite countrywide protest from July 1, demanding the repeal of the Viksit
Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G).
The VB-G RAM G scheme will come into force on July 1, replacing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural
Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), launched by the Congress-led UPA government in 2006. According
to the notification, the revised national average wage has now increased from ₹298.8 per day
under MGNREGA to ₹327.4 per day under VB-G RAM G, an average increase of ₹28.6 per day. It said 21
states and administrative units have been brought up to the new ₹300 interim base wage rate, while states
including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Assam will see wage increases in the range of 15
per cent to 25 per cent. Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland will see the highest percentage increase of nearly 24.5
per cent, it added.

The government said the revised wage structure has been designed to ensure that the greatest gains accrue to
states that historically had lower wage rates. It added that states with higher existing wage rates have also
received upward revisions, with Haryana having a notified wage rate of ₹409, Goa ₹406, Kerala ₹401 and
Sikkim's high-altitude gram panchayats ₹450 per day.
Source- https://www.livemint.com/news/india/vbg-ram-g-act-to-come-into-force-on-july-1-revised-wages-

LEGAL REASONING

I. Article 131 of the Constitution of India provides that the Supreme Court shall have exclusive and original
jurisdiction in any dispute: The intention of the Constitution makers is that such disputes should not be
subjected to several tiers of the judicial hierarchy, but should come, for once and for all, before the highest court
of the land.
(a) between the Government of India and one or more States;
(b) between Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other;
(c) between two or more States if and in so far as the dispute involves any question (whether of law or fact) on
which the existence or extent of a legal right depends.
The dispute between the Union of India and the State cannot but be a dispute which arises out of the difference
between the Government in office at the Centre and the Government in office in the State. But there is a further
prerequisite which narrows down the ambit of the class of disputes which fall within Article 131. That
requirement is that the dispute must involve a question whether of law or fact, on which the existence or extent
of a legal right depends. It is this qualification which contains the true guide for determining whether a
particular dispute is comprehended within Art. 131. Mere wrangles between Governments have no place in the
scheme of that Article. The purpose of Art. 131 is to afford a forum for the resolution of disputes which depend
for their decision on the existence or extent of a legal right. The intention of the Constitution makers is that such
disputes should not be subjected to several tiers of the judicial hierarchy, but should come, for once and for all,
before the highest court of the land. It is only when a legal, not a mere political, issue arises touching upon the
existence or extent of a legal right that Article 131 is attracted.
In the case of Tashi Delek Gaming Solutions Ltd v State of Karnataka, the lottery agents of the States Sikkim
and Meghalaya challenged the banning of lottery games by the State of Karnataka. The Karnataka High Court
held that this dispute held the legal rights of all the three States; hence, the remedy will be under article 131
only. But the Supreme Court held otherwise and said that these agents were given the right to represent the State
Governments and hence, were private parties, thus, not coming under the jurisdiction of article 131. Such an
agent had the right to sue and be sued in his own name and thus, it would not come under this article 131.

The Mullaperiyar dam issue is a longstanding dispute between two Indian states - Kerala and Tamil
Nadu. The dam is located in Kerala's Idukki district on the Periyar river. There have been fresh disputes
on sharing of Cauvery water between Tamil Nadu and Kerala and the formation of the Cauvery Water
Management Authority. In recent years, increasing water scarcity, a rapid rise in urban and rural
demands for freshwater, and contentious political dynamics have further exacerbated the problem.
Owing to continuous interstate water dispute, the state of Kerala decided to file a petition in the High
Court of Kerala.
options:
The State of Kerala can file a petition in the High Court of Kerala as the Mullaperiyar dam is situated in
Kerala and hence, the jurisdiction lies with the High Court of Kerala.

The State of Kerala cannot file a petition in the High Court of Kerala as it does not have Original Jurisdiction
over it since the original jurisdiction for the dispute between the states lie with the Supreme Court.

River water disputes being important disputes between two or more States and/or the Union, should be heard
by a more competent court.

The State of Kerala should directly file a petition in the Supreme Court as it is the highest judicial court and
can solve the dispute efficiently.

The Government of Palampur declared the State to be a free zone from online and internet lotteries and
prohibited the sale of all computerized and online lottery tickets marketed and operated through vending

Because of the recent notification passed by the state of Palampur, the states incurred heavy losses.

Both (A) and (C).

Mr. Muskesh Narangi, a politician from the Janta Party, is the Prime Minister of Sindhustan, a
country in South Asia having the same Constitution as that of India. Janta Party wanted to win the
upcoming election in Bengal, a state in Sindhustan. But the Janta Party lost the elections to another
party, CPP. A false memo accusing the CM of Bengal of corruption, nepotism and favouritism was
submitted by the opposition members of the Janta Party. In furtherance of the memo, the Union
Government appointed a one-man commission to inquire into the allegations levelled against the Chief
Minister. State Government of Bengal filed a petition under Art. 131 of the Constitution challenging the
authority and legality of the said commission. Is the suit maintainable?
options:
The present petition doesn't qualify under Art. 131 as there has been no actual cause of action and the present
scenario doesn't fit the criterion established in Art. 131.

The dispute involves a question of law or fact that transcends any statutory or constitutional rights and hence,
is maintainable under Article 131.

The allegations made by the plaintiff is merely a political propaganda and no question of law or legal rights
are involved and hence, the petition is not maintainable under Article 131.
As the dispute involves the Centre and the State, the suit falls under the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

II. A recent rule in company law has generated concerns and criticism regarding the requirement for
independent directors (IDs) to clear an online proficiency test conducted by the Indian Institute of Corporate
Affairs (IICA). This rule mandates that existing IDs and individuals aspiring to become IDs must pass the self-
assessment test within a year of their inclusion in the IICA's maintained data. To recognize the standing and
experience of individuals, the rule exempts directors or key managerial personnel who have worked in these
roles for at least ten years in listed or unlisted companies. While there is no limit on the number of attempts to
clear the test, a minimum aggregate score of 60% is necessary.
At first glance, this move seems reasonable. The rule introduces the concept of passing a test to formally qualify
and demonstrate the expected qualifications for individuals aspiring to be IDs, which is already provided by the
Companies Act, 2013. The existing regulations under the Companies Act outline certain qualifications for IDs,
including their experience and knowledge in relevant fields such as finance, law, management, sales, marketing,
administration, research, corporate governance, and technical operations related to the company's business.
Additionally, IDs are obligated by law to regularly update and refresh their skills, knowledge, and familiarity
with the company. Thus, the Companies Act already requires a minimum set of qualifications for IDs. However,
despite these provisions, some concerns have emerged.
Certain industry bodies, chambers, and even IDs themselves are contemplating recommending to the Ministry
of Corporate Affairs that this rule be reconsidered. Their concern stems from the belief that it is inappropriate to
expect IDs, who are often individuals of reputation, standing, and experience, and who meet the legal eligibility
criteria for ID appointments, to undergo and pass a technical test to establish their eligibility. They argue that
this requirement could undermine their status and position.
Critics point out that the Companies Act already has stringent eligibility criteria for IDs, as it states that only
individuals considered by the board of directors to possess integrity, relevant expertise, and experience should
be appointed as IDs. According to them, this requirement is sufficient to ensure suitable individuals are selected,
rendering an additional test unnecessary. Hence, their view is that this rule should be revoked. While this
argument is intriguing, there is no inherent issue with passing a test to establish proficiency. Another argument
raised is that no such test requirement exists for other directors, so why should it be imposed on IDs. While it is
true that other directors are not required to pass such a test, it cannot be denied that the roles, duties, and
responsibilities of IDs are significantly greater than those of other directors. It is prudent for IDs to establish
their eligibility by passing a simple test. In fact, IDs and their conduct play critical roles in adhering to corporate
governance norms.
The new rule in company law regarding the proficiency test for IDs has sparked concerns and criticism. While
some argue that IDs should not be required to undergo such a test, considering their reputation and eligibility
under the existing law, others believe that passing the test is a reasonable way to establish proficiency. IDs hold
crucial positions in corporate governance, and the test can help ensure their qualifications and capabilities align


with their responsibilities. Ultimately, the debate continues regarding whether the rule should be maintained or
reconsidered.
Source: https://taxguru.in/company-law/independent-director-section1496-companies-act-2013.html
content.questionText:
Ms. Sharma has been an independent director at 'TechFlow Ltd.", a listed company, for the past 12
years. Recently, she was notified about the new rule that requires IDs to clear an online proficiency test
conducted by the IICA. Given her long-standing role in the company, she was surprised and contacted
the legal team for advice. In this context, should Ms. Sharma be required to take the proficiency test as
per the new rule?
options:
Yes, because as an Independent Director, Ms. Sharma is obligated to regularly update and refresh her skills,
knowledge, and familiarity with the company, which the proficiency test seeks to establish.

No, because Ms. Sharma, as a director, has served for more than ten years in a listed company, making her
exempt from the test under the new rule.

Yes, because the proficiency test aims to demonstrate the expected qualifications for individuals aspiring to
be IDs, which Ms. Sharma must prove despite her experience.

No, because Ms. Sharma, as an existing ID, has already demonstrated her proficiency and capabilities
through her past work, making the test unnecessary for her.

Mr. Bhattacharya, a seasoned finance professional, has never served as a director or in a key
managerial role in a company. With over 15 years of experience in the finance sector and having
consulted for multiple firms on financial strategy, he aspires to serve as an Independent Director. He is

Yes, because the Companies Act, 2013 requires a proficiency test for Independent Directors.

III. Article 352 of the Constitution provides for the provision of National Emergency which can be applied if
any extraordinary situation arises that may threaten the security, peace, stability and governance of the country.
Whenever any of the following grounds occur, an emergency can be imposed: War, External aggression; or
Internal rebellion. Article 352 provides that if the President is ‘satisfied’ on the grounds that the security of India
is threatened due to outside aggression or armed rebellion, he can issue a proclamation to that effect regarding
the whole of India or a part thereof. However, sub-clause (3) states that when a piece of written advice is given
by the Union Cabinet then only the President can make such a proclamation. Such a proclamation must be
placed before each house of the Parliament and must be approved within one month of the declaration of the
proclamation otherwise it will expire.
Furthermore, it is not necessary that for the proclamation of National Emergency, external aggression or armed
rebellion should actually happen. Even if there is a possibility that such a situation can arise, a National
Emergency can be proclaimed. If the situation improves then the President can revoke the emergency through
another proclamation. The President may make a Proclamation of Emergency in respect of the whole India or
any part of India, as required.
If approved by both Houses of Parliament, then National Emergency can continue for 6 months and it can be
renewed by approval of Parliament after every 6 months. But if the dissolution of Lok Sabha takes place in that
6 months and resolution for renewal of National Emergency is under consideration then emergency exists till 30
days from the first sitting of newly elected LS provided that it is approved by Rajya Sabha.
According to Article 353, the Union can use its executive power to the extent of giving directions to the State
relating to the manner in which the executive powers shall be exercised by the State. As per Article 353(b), the
Union Parliament can make laws relating to the matters in the State List. According to Article 354, the
distribution of revenue between the Union and the State can be altered by the Centre. As per Article 358, during
a National Emergency, the fundamental rights under Article 19 shall be suspended. However, in any case, the
fundamental rights under Article 20 and Article 21 will not be affected.
Source- https://blog.ipleaders.in/emergency-india/

IV. By the 42nd Amendment of the Constitution, adopted in 1976, Fundamental Duties of the citizens have also
been enumerated. Article 51A, contained in Part IV A of the Constitution deals with Fundamental Duties. They

are not enforceable in Courts but must be harmonized with Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of
State Policy. There can be laws made to give effect to the Fundamental Duties if they are in consonance with
Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy. These enjoin upon a citizen among other things, to
abide by the Constitution, to cherish and follow noble ideals, which inspired India's struggle for freedom, to
defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so, and to promote harmony and spirit of
common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities.
Article 51A. Fundamental Duties.—It shall be the duty of every citizen of India—(a) to abide by the
Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; (b) to cherish
and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom; (c) to uphold and protect the
sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (d) to defend the country and render national service when called upon
to do so; (e) to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India
transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the
dignity of women; (f) to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; (g) to protect and
improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living
creatures; (h) to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; (i) to safeguard
public property and to abjure violence; (j) to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective
activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement; (k) who is a parent or
guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six
and fourteen years.
Source: https://knowindia.india.gov.in/profile/fundamental-duties.php

V. A geographical indication (GI) is a sign used on products that have a specific geographical origin and possess
qualities or a reputation that are due to that origin. In order to function as a GI, a sign must identify a product as
originating in a given place. In addition, the qualities, characteristics or reputation of the product should be
essentially due to the place of origin. Since the qualities depend on the geographical place of production, there
is a clear link between the product and its original place of production.
As per section 2 (e) of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the
definition is as follows:
(e) "geographical indication", in relation to goods, means an indication which identifies such goods as
agricultural goods, natural goods or manufactured goods as originating, or manufactured in the territory of a
country, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such
goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and in case where such goods are manufactured goods
one of the activities of either the production or of processing or preparation of the goods concerned takes place
in such territory, region or locality, as the case may be.
Section 2 (f) states: "goods" means any agricultural, natural or manufactured goods or any goods of handicraft
or of industry and includes food stuff.
Section 2 (k) "producer", in relation to goods, means any person who: (i) if such goods are agricultural goods,
produces the goods and includes the person who processes or packages such goods; (ii) if such goods are natural
goods, exploits the goods; (iii) if such goods are handicraft or industrial goods, makes or manufactures the
goods, and includes any person who trades or deals in such production, exploitation, making or manufacturing,
as the case may be, of the goods.
A geographical indication must be registered by a producer with the registrar of Geographical indications after
paying the mandatory fee. The registration of a geographical indication shall be for a period of ten years, but
may be renewed from time to time according to section 18. As per section 20, no person shall be entitled to
institute any proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of an unregistered or lapsed


geographical indication. There can be infringement action in registered GI under section 21 and 22. There will
be penalty as fine and imprisonment if false geographical indication is applied.
Source: https://ipindia.gov.in/act-1999.htm and
https://www.wipo.int/geo_indications/en/#:~:text=A%20geographical%20indication%20(GI)%20is,originating
%20in%20a%20given%20place.

No, because the registration has surpassed the time period with no renewal.

VI. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is a comprehensive piece of legislation that governs the admissibility and
relevancy of evidence in the Indian court system. The Act is divided into three parts: Part 1 deals with the
relevancy of facts, Part 2 covers types of evidence and when each is preferred, and Part 3 focuses on issues such
as the burden of proof and estoppel. For this excerpt, we will delve into the Doctrine of Estoppel as outlined in
Section 115 and 116 of the Act, which provides numerous legal principles that can be tested in various
hypothetical scenarios.
Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act defines the doctrine of Estoppel. It states, "When one person has, by his
declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true by his
act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between
himself and such person or his representative, to deny the truth of that thing".
   1. Principle of Representation: A representation must be made by one person to another. This
      representation must concern an existing fact and be conveyed in a manner that makes the other person
      believe it to be true.
   2. Principle of Reliance: The person to whom the representation is made must act upon their belief of its
      truthfulness. If this person suffers a loss due to their reliance on the representation, the doctrine of
      estoppel may apply.
   3. Principle of Consistency: One cannot contradict, deny or declare to be false a previous statement made
      by them in court. For example, if a person accepts their liability to make payment under an arbitration
      award, they cannot later challenge the award.
   4. Principle of Legitimacy: A person is bound by their previous statements and cannot challenge facts
      they've previously accepted. In Shammim Beg v. Najmunnissa Begum, the husband could not challenge
      the legitimacy of a child he had accepted as his own.


Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act extends the doctrine of estoppel to specific circumstances involving
tenancies and licenses. This section prohibits a tenant or licensee from denying the title of the landlord or
licensor during the continuance of the tenancy or license.
   5. Principle of Tenancy: No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall,
      during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the
      beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property.
   6. Principle of License: No person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in
      possession thereof, shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time
      when such license was given.
These principles are interrelated and form the bedrock of the Doctrine of Estoppel in Indian law, ensuring that
individuals cannot benefit from their own deceit or contradiction in legal proceedings.
[Source with edits revision made from: https://lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-pg/notes-on-introduction-to-
indian-evidence-act/]
content.questionText:
A person applies for a loan from a bank based on the representation of his friend that he owns a house
worth 50 lakhs and that he is willing to mortgage it as a security for the loan. The bank sanctions the loan
and disburses the amount to the person. Later, the person defaults on the loan repayment and the bank
tries to recover the money by enforcing the mortgage. However, it turns out that the house belongs to
someone else and the friend had forged the ownership documents. The bank files a suit against the friend
for fraud and misrepresentation. Can the friend invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the bank from
suing him?
options:
No, because he made a false representation of an existing fact to the bank, which acted upon it and suffered a
loss, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the bank, but only to his friend, who was not a party to the
suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

Yes, because he made a representation in good faith and without any intention to deceive the bank, which
acted upon it at its own risk, and he cannot be held liable for any loss.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact, which was contingent on his ability to acquire the
house, and he cannot be estopped by a fact that did not materialize.

content.questionText:
A person rents a shop from another person for a period of one year. The rent agreement mentions that
the landlord has a valid title to the shop and that the tenant will not dispute it during the tenancy. After
six months, the tenant learns that the landlord has mortgaged the shop to a bank and that the bank has
initiated foreclosure proceedings against the landlord. The tenant stops paying rent and files a suit for
injunction against the landlord and the bank, claiming that he has a better title to the shop than the
owner. Can the tenant invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the landlord and the bank from evicting
him?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he agreed to the landlord's title) to the
landlord, who acted upon it and leased him the shop, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact (that he would not dispute the landlord's title) to the
landlord, who acted upon it and leased him the shop, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the bank, but only to the landlord, who was not a party to
the suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

No, because he accepted a fact (that the landlord had a title to the shop) in his rent agreement, and then tried
to deny it during the continuance of the tenancy, and he cannot be estopped by his own acceptance.

A person obtains a license from another person to use their vacant land for parking his car. The
license is for a period of six months and the person pays a monthly fee to the licensor. After three months,
the licensor sells the land to a third party, who wants to construct a building on it. The third party asks
the person to vacate the land and stop parking his car there. The person refuses and files a suit for
injunction against the third party, claiming that the original licensor had no valid title of ownership. Can
the person invoke the doctrine of estoppel to prevent the third party?
options:
Yes, because he made a representation of an existing fact (that he had a license to use the land) to the third
party, who acted upon it and bought the land, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

Yes, because he made a representation of a future fact (that he would use the land for parking his car) to the
licensor, who acted upon it and granted him the license, and he cannot deny the truth of that fact.

No, because he did not make any representation to the licensor or the third party, but only obtained a license
from the licensor, who was not a party to the suit, and he cannot be estopped by a third party.

No, because he obtained a license from the licensor to use their immovable property, and then relied on it to
claim some right or interest in the property, and he cannot be estopped by his own reliance.

      estoppel may apply.

      by them in court. For example, if a person accepts their liability to make payment under an arbitration

VII. Res means subject matter and judicata means adjudged or decided and together it means ‘a matter
adjudged’. In simpler words, the thing has been judged by the court, the issue before a court has already been
decided by another court and between the same parties. Hence, the subsequent court will dismiss the case as it
has been decided by another court. Res judicata applies to both civil and criminal legal systems. No suit which
has been directly or indirectly tried in a former suit can be tried again. The principle of res judicata seeks to
promote the fair administration of justice and honesty and to prevent the law from abuse. The principle of res
judicata applies when a litigant attempts to file a subsequent lawsuit on the same matter, after having received a
judgment in a previous case involving the same parties. In many jurisdictions, this applies not only to the
specific claims made in the first case but also to claims that could have been made during the same case. The
double jeopardy provision of the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protects people from being put on a
second trial after the case has been judged. So the doctrine of res judicata addresses this issue and it bars any
party to retry a judgment once it has been decided. Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Court incorporates the
doctrine of res judicata also known as ‘rule of conclusiveness of judgment’. The doctrine of res judicata and res
sub judice varies in some factors such as (a). Res sub judice applies to a matter that is pending trial whereas res
judicata applies to a matter adjudicated or arbitrated and (b) Res sub judice prohibits the trial of a suit that has a
pending decision in a previous suit i.e., the suit is still not finally decided, whereas res judicata prohibits the trial
of a suit that has been decided in a former suit.
Source: https://blog.ipleaders.in/overview-on-doctrine-of-res-judicata/

LOGICAL REASONING

I. Firstly, Karnataka has had a history and tradition of ‘Centrist’ politics, with the state policies being mainly left
of centre, which is generally pro-poor and socialist to a large extent. Although Mahatma Gandhi and Karl Marx
have had their share of influence in the past, a more abiding influence has been that of liberal democrats like
Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar and socialists such as Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan, and his
bitter opponent Indira Gandhi, who too adopted socialist policies when pushed to a corner. Those influenced by
the socialist thought of Lohia were men like Shantaveri Gopala Gowda, K.H. Ranganath, J.H. Patel, S.R.
Bommai, Ramakrishna Hegde and of course, Devaraj Urs who carried out the most significant Land Reforms
Act. Even H.D. Deve Gowda, who grew up in the same political milieu, is undoubtedly committed to socialism
and secularism, though his son is bereft of any such commitment to ideals. Fourthly, Karnataka has had an
intellectual movement inspired by liberal, secular and universalist ideas prominent in the poetry of
Gopalkrishna Adiga, D.R. Bendre and Kuvempu. In the field of literature, it was evident in the writings of U.R.
Anantmurthy, Girish Karnad and in the journalism of P. Lankesh, which was carried forward by his daughter
Gauri Lankesh till she was killed for her stubborn courage. Fifthly, there was an important movement led by
rationalists and critical thinkers who exposed godmen, myths, mythologies and superstitions, such as Abraham
Kovoor and H. Narasimhaiah, then Vice Chancellor of Bangalore University in the mid-1970s. We also had
M.M. Kalburgi, Vice Chancellor of Hampi University, a great rationalist who was killed in August 2015 by
people opposing rationalism and a questioning mind. To recall their contribution today is very important when
fake news, prejudice, superstition, bigotry and hate speeches are the common currency of politics.
Sixth, caste politics have been a far more important factor than religion-based politics. Unlike religion, caste is
not seen as an exclusionary or divisive factor in our politics. It is seen as an aggregator or a mobilising force for
leaders who promote policies of social justice for their constituents. Finally, Karnataka has had a long tradition
of Dalit protests led by ‘Bandaya’ and ‘Andolan’ movements that have shaped our political, social and literary
sensibilities. No politician can afford to ignore the power of the suppressed.

content.passageText:
LOGICAL REASONING

I. Firstly, Karnataka has had a history and tradition of ‘Centrist’ politics, with the state policies being mainly left
of centre, which is generally pro-poor and socialist to a large extent. Although Mahatma Gandhi and Karl Marx
have had their share of influence in the past, a more abiding influence has been that of liberal democrats like
Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar and socialists such as Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan, and his
bitter opponent Indira Gandhi, who too adopted socialist policies when pushed to a corner. Those influenced by
the socialist thought of Lohia were men like Shantaveri Gopala Gowda, K.H. Ranganath, J.H. Patel, S.R.
Bommai, Ramakrishna Hegde and of course, Devaraj Urs who carried out the most significant Land Reforms
Act. Even H.D. Deve Gowda, who grew up in the same political milieu, is undoubtedly committed to socialism
and secularism, though his son is bereft of any such commitment to ideals. Fourthly, Karnataka has had an
intellectual movement inspired by liberal, secular and universalist ideas prominent in the poetry of
Gopalkrishna Adiga, D.R. Bendre and Kuvempu. In the field of literature, it was evident in the writings of U.R.
Anantmurthy, Girish Karnad and in the journalism of P. Lankesh, which was carried forward by his daughter
Gauri Lankesh till she was killed for her stubborn courage. Fifthly, there was an important movement led by
rationalists and critical thinkers who exposed godmen, myths, mythologies and superstitions, such as Abraham
Kovoor and H. Narasimhaiah, then Vice Chancellor of Bangalore University in the mid-1970s. We also had
M.M. Kalburgi, Vice Chancellor of Hampi University, a great rationalist who was killed in August 2015 by
people opposing rationalism and a questioning mind. To recall their contribution today is very important when
fake news, prejudice, superstition, bigotry and hate speeches are the common currency of politics.
Sixth, caste politics have been a far more important factor than religion-based politics. Unlike religion, caste is
not seen as an exclusionary or divisive factor in our politics. It is seen as an aggregator or a mobilising force for
leaders who promote policies of social justice for their constituents. Finally, Karnataka has had a long tradition
of Dalit protests led by ‘Bandaya’ and ‘Andolan’ movements that have shaped our political, social and literary
sensibilities. No politician can afford to ignore the power of the suppressed.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from A Vote Against ‘40% Commission’, ‘Double Engine Sarkar’
and the Politics of Hindutva, The Wire https://thewire.in/politics/a-vote-against-40-commission-double-engine-

II. Throughout an unusually sunny Fall in 1970, hundreds of students and faculty at Syracuse University sat one
at a time before a printing computer terminal (similar to an electric typewriter) connected to an IBM 360
mainframe located across campus in New York state. Almost none of them had ever used a computer before, let
alone a computer-based information retrieval system. Their hands trembled as they touched the keyboard;
several later reported that they had been afraid of breaking the entire system as they typed.
The participants were performing their first online searches, entering carefully chosen words to find relevant
psychology abstracts in a brand-new database. They typed one key term or instruction per line, like ‘Motivation’
in line 1, ‘Esteem’ in line 2, and 'L1 and L2' in line 3 in order to search for papers that included both terms.
After running the query, the terminal produced a printout indicating how many documents matched each search;
users could then narrow down or expand that search before generating a list of article citations. Many users
burst into laughter upon seeing the response from a computer so far away.
As part of a telephone survey afterwards, participants were asked to provide two or three words describing the
experience. Of the 78 total words provided, 21 were the same adjective: ‘frustrating’. Participants had trouble
signing on to the system and experienced unpredictable failures, ‘irrelevant output’ and, most of all, not
knowing ‘what words to use in a search’. Yet they also found the system intriguing and exciting (‘fun’,
‘thorough’, ‘I dig computers’), and 94 per cent said they would use SUPARS (the Syracuse University
Psychological Abstracts Retrieval Service) again if it were available. Several offered to keep the experiment
running past its deadline by asking their departments to contribute funding to the project.
This group of academic guinea pigs, mostly graduate students in education, psychology and librarianship, were


part of a radical online search experiment run by the Syracuse University School of Library Science. SUPARS
was one of many ambitious information-retrieval studies that took place between the late 1960s and mid-1970s
on US university campuses. A number of factors led to the surge in this research. Developments in computer-
processing capability for speed and storage had allowed academic databases and catalogues to be digitised and
moved online. Computer terminals were newly modular and could be placed around campuses for decentralised
access to mainframes. And military and industry funding for computer-based research was more abundant than
it had ever been. Given the opportunity, academic librarians took advantage of the chance to explore this
expensive new technology. In turn, universities offered unclassified environments for collaborations with
corporate technology firms and military groups; SUPARS was sponsored by the Rome Air Development Center,
the laboratory arm of the US Air Force.
Source: Ingenious librarians, Aeon
https://aeon.co/essays/the-1970s-librarians-who-revolutionised-the-challenge-of-search

V. The ethics of virtue emerges as a normative moral theory, fundamentally concerned with the cultivation of
moral agents capable of judicious decision-making. This theory, often attributed to Aristotelian thought, posits
that humans are uniquely deserving of moral consideration due to their capacity for ethical cognition. It is this
very capacity that distinguishes Homo sapiens from other sentient beings, thereby justifying speciesism as a
morally relevant criterion. Aristotle's conceptualization of human nature as inherently moral and intellectual
serves as the bedrock for ethical knowledge, which he argues is indispensable for virtuous conduct.
Contrastingly, deontological ethics, championed by Emmanuel Kant, adheres to an unwavering categorical
imperative that proscribes certain actions irrespective of their consequences. This ethical rigidity can sometimes
yield morally untenable outcomes. Utilitarianism, as espoused by Stuart Mill and Bentham, offers a
consequentialist counterpoint, prioritizing the aggregate well-being of the majority, albeit at the risk of ethical
excesses.
The ethics of virtue finds resonance in diverse philosophical traditions, including Buddhism and ancient Greek
thought. Unlike deontological and consequentialist ethics, which focus on moral norms and outcomes
respectively, virtue ethics centers on the cultivation of moral character. Care ethicists diverge slightly,
emphasizing the relational aspects of morality, but their approach suffers from limitations such as parochialism
and essentialism. Aristotle's virtue ethics, grounded in rational consciousness, offers a more robust framework.
In the context of social justice, figures like Robin Hood challenge Aristotelian virtue ethics by advocating for
redistributive actions that may be considered immoral in isolation but contribute to greater societal well-being.


This tension between individual morality and collective justice underscores the complexities inherent in ethical
reasoning.
The rationalist perspective on ethics often engenders skepticism towards socialization-based explanations,
questioning the adequacy of internalized norms in accounting for individual moral agency. Aristotle and Plato,
both seminal figures in Western philosophy, offer nuanced understandings of the political community as a space
for the realization of virtue and justice. Aristotle's concept of Eudaimonism and Plato's ideal state both aim at
harmonizing individual and collective interests, thereby elevating the discourse on ethics and politics to an
ontological plane.
In summation, ethics is not merely a prescriptive set of norms but a complex interplay of individual agency,
collective well-being, and rational deliberation. It is an expression of human power, realized through the
intricate dynamics of ethical cognition and social relations. Freedom, in this context, is not an abstract ideal but
a tangible manifestation of ethical power, achieved through the conscientious navigation of moral complexities.

ENGLISH

I. Atanu Ghosh is a storyteller who explores the power of fairy tales to convey unhappy truths while holding up
the possibility of a happy outcome. His latest film, Aaro Ek Prithibi, is an original story fashioned from
contemporary lived-in experience. It is a post-colonial noir that uncovers a London that Bengali cinema and the
Bengali spectator have not explored. In Ghosh's noir-meets-fairy-tale, unrespectable people prove to be good
Samaritans, and he impels us to re-adjust our assessment of the bases of human bonding. Ghosh's stories are not
intended or contrived to look agentic. Women in his stories are not equated with greed for the good life but
instead are portrayed as they make their way through the plot of life.

Ghosh's art of storytelling is fluid, central to the cinematic flanerie that best describes his style. He is the quietly
watchful flaneur around the city and a little beyond, peering underneath the otherwise placid carpet of normality
with a gaze that is both piercing and humorous. His stories challenge us to rethink what we know about
ourselves and others, how our everyday differentiation between familiar and strange, known and alien, right and
wrong comes crashing down in crisis situations.
Ghosh's cinematography is a delicate visual construct, distinct in its use of light and darkness, indoors and
outdoors. If the change of light helps map the transitions, then the measured, restrained sound track, complete
with some deeply evocative lyrics, preserves the free flow.
Aaro Ek Prithibi pulls off a post-colonial noir by uncovering a London that Bengali cinema and the Bengali
spectator have not explored. Ghosh peels away all the glitz of the erstwhile capital of a far-flung Empire and
destabilizes the fantasies that fuel the desires that in turn sustain the NRI dream.

In the end, Aaro Ek Prithibi brings together essentially two worldviews: the one privileges truth-seeking as a
rational enterprise and the other foregrounds affective truth, with its less concrete but not necessarily shakier
moorings in faith, love, hope, compassion, and goodness.

Ghosh continues to find fresh stories and faces within the seemingly limited, unsensationally quotidian circle of
life that is urban, middle- and upper-middle-class Kolkata. Each new story inspires him to stretch his cinematic
art little by little to accommodate these ever-expanding worlds enlivened by his ever-expansive world-view.

II. In the world of technology, the race to be first is often seen as the key to success. After all, the first company
to bring a new technology to market is usually the one that shapes the product definitions and sets the standard
for everyone else to follow. However, in today's fast-paced business environment, being the first to market is no
longer enough. Instead, the biggest payoffs often go to companies that can successfully develop integrated
approaches for mass production and distribution.
A prime example of this phenomenon can be seen in the history of videocassette recorders (VCRs). In 1975,
producers of the Beta format were the first to bring VCRs to the commercial market. However, their rivals,


producers of the VHS (Video Home System) format, proved to be more successful at forming strategic alliances
with other producers and distributors to manufacture and market their VCR format. This allowed VHS to
quickly gain a dominant position in the global VCR market, despite Beta's substantial technological head start.

While Beta may have been the first to market, their reluctance to form strategic alliances eventually cost them
the competition. By seeking to maintain exclusive control over VCR distribution, they lost ground to VHS,
which was able to form alliances and secure a greater market share. Even though VHS was not technically
superior or cheaper than Beta, they quickly turned their slight early lead in sales into a dominant position.
One factor that contributed to VHS's success was their strategic alignments with producers of prerecorded tapes.
This reinforced their advantage and expanded their market share, as consumers perceived that prerecorded tapes
were more available in VHS format. By the end of the 1980s, Beta was no longer in production, and VHS had
become the dominant VCR format.

This example illustrates the importance of not only being the first to market but also having a comprehensive
strategy for mass production and distribution. Companies that are able to successfully integrate these elements
are more likely to come out on top in the long run. It's not enough to simply have a great product or technology;
it's essential to have a plan for how to get it into the hands of consumers.

Today's rapidly changing business environment means that companies must be agile and adaptable. The ability
to form strategic alliances, work collaboratively with other companies, and rapidly scale production and
distribution are all critical components of success. While being the first to market may offer a brief advantage,
it's ultimately the companies that can successfully develop and execute an integrated approach that will come
out on top.

II. In the world of technology, the race to be first is often seen as the key to success. After all, the first company
to bring a new technology to market is usually the one that shapes the product definitions and sets the standard
for everyone else to follow. However, in today's fast-paced business environment, being the first to market is no
longer enough. Instead, the biggest payoffs often go to companies that can successfully develop integrated
approaches for mass production and distribution.
A prime example of this phenomenon can be seen in the history of videocassette recorders (VCRs). In 1975,
producers of the Beta format were the first to bring VCRs to the commercial market. However, their rivals,


producers of the VHS (Video Home System) format, proved to be more successful at forming strategic alliances
with other producers and distributors to manufacture and market their VCR format. This allowed VHS to
quickly gain a dominant position in the global VCR market, despite Beta's substantial technological head start.

While Beta may have been the first to market, their reluctance to form strategic alliances eventually cost them
the competition. By seeking to maintain exclusive control over VCR distribution, they lost ground to VHS,
which was able to form alliances and secure a greater market share. Even though VHS was not technically
superior or cheaper than Beta, they quickly turned their slight early lead in sales into a dominant position.
One factor that contributed to VHS's success was their strategic alignments with producers of prerecorded tapes.
This reinforced their advantage and expanded their market share, as consumers perceived that prerecorded tapes
were more available in VHS format. By the end of the 1980s, Beta was no longer in production, and VHS had
become the dominant VCR format.

This example illustrates the importance of not only being the first to market but also having a comprehensive
strategy for mass production and distribution. Companies that are able to successfully integrate these elements
are more likely to come out on top in the long run. It's not enough to simply have a great product or technology;
it's essential to have a plan for how to get it into the hands of consumers.

to form strategic alliances, work collaboratively with other companies, and rapidly scale production and
distribution are all critical components of success. While being the first to market may offer a brief advantage,
it's ultimately the companies that can successfully develop and execute an integrated approach that will come
out on top.

III. Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican-born social activist, arrived in the United States in 1916, at a time when the
country was experiencing significant social upheaval. The return of African American soldiers from the First
World War in 1918 created a ripe environment for Garvey's message of unity, pride, and improved conditions
for African American communities. These soldiers, who had fought bravely for their country, returned home to a
United States that was as segregated as it had been before the war. This disconnect between expectations and
reality, according to anthropologist Anthony F. C. Wallace, can inspire a revitalization movement. In this case,
the movement was an organized, conscious effort to construct a culture that fulfilled longstanding expectations.

Garvey's message resonated deeply with African American communities across the country. He advocated for a
"back-to-Africa" movement, which aimed to promote black pride and self-sufficiency by creating an
independent black nation in Africa. This message was particularly appealing to those who were disillusioned
with the status quo and were looking for a new way forward. Garvey's ideas provided a sense of hope and
direction to those who had been marginalized and oppressed for generations.
Some scholars have argued that Garvey created the consciousness from which he built the largest revitalization
movement in African American history in the 1920s. However, others believe that Garvey merely gave voice to
a consciousness of identity, strength, and sense of history that already existed within the African American
community. Regardless of where one falls on this debate, there is no denying the impact that Garvey had on the
African American community.

Garvey's movement was unique in that it emphasized a sense of pride and self-sufficiency, rather than relying
on the goodwill of the white majority. This was a radical departure from the prevailing narrative of the time,
which suggested that African Americans should seek to assimilate into white society. Garvey's message was one
of empowerment, and it resonated deeply with those who had been marginalized and oppressed for generations.


Despite the many challenges that Garvey and his movement faced, including opposition from the government
and internal divisions, his ideas continued to spread. He founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association
(UNIA), which grew to become one of the largest and most influential organizations in African American
history. Through the UNIA, Garvey advocated for economic and political self-sufficiency, and his ideas inspired
generations of African American activists.

Today, Marcus Garvey is remembered as a pioneering figure in the struggle for African American civil rights.
His message of pride, unity, and self-sufficiency continues to resonate with communities across the country, and
his impact can be felt in the ongoing fight for racial justice and equality.

IV. Choosing the perfect gift can be a difficult task. When in doubt, flowers and fruits are always acceptable
presents. Flowers are a proud assertion of beauty and a contrast to the somewhat stern countenance of ordinary
nature. They serve as a reminder that a ray of beauty outvalues all the utilities of the world. Fruits are the flower
of commodities and can have fantastic values attached to them.

For more common gifts, necessity makes pertinences and beauty every day. It is always satisfying to supply
basic necessities like bread and water. Necessity does everything well, and in our condition of universal
dependence, it is heroic to let the petitioner be the judge of his necessity and to give all that is asked, even if it is
inconvenient. However, fantastic desires should be left to the office of punishing them by others.

A gift should properly belong to the recipient's character and be easily associated with them in thought. Tokens
of compliment and love can often be barbarous. The only true gift is a portion of oneself. It restores society to a
point where a person's biography is conveyed in their gift. It is also an index of one's merit. The poet brings his
poem, the shepherd his lamb, the farmer his corn, the miner his gem, the sailor his coral and shells, the painter
his picture, and the girl a handkerchief of her own sewing.

Buying gifts can be a lifeless business. It is fit for kings and rich men who represent kings, but not for those
who wish to give a portion of themselves. While giving gifts can be difficult, receiving them can be even harder.
We are either glad or sorry at a gift, and both emotions are unbecoming. It is degrading to rejoice or grieve at a
gift. When a gift pleases us too much, we should be ashamed that the donor should read our hearts and see that
we love their commodity, not them.

The gift should be the flowing of the giver unto the recipient, correspondent to the recipient's flowing unto the
giver. When the waters are at level, then the goods pass from one to the other. Gratitude should not be expected,
as it is continually punished by the insensibility of the obliged person. Being served is a very onerous business,
and the debtor naturally wishes to give you a slap.

V. If it were necessary to trench further upon the field of morals, it might be suggested that the dogma of
equality applied only within the limits of ordinary dealings. You cannot deal with someone, where both are free
to choose, except on the footing of equal treatment and the same rules for both. The ever-growing value set
upon peace and the social relations tends to give the law of social being the appearance of the law of all being.
But it seems clear to me that the ultima ratio, not only of rulers but of private persons, is force, and at the
bottom of all private relations, however tempered by sympathy and social feelings, is a justifiable self-
preference. If a man is on a plank in the deep sea that will only float one, and a stranger lays hold of it, he will
thrust him off if he can. When the state finds itself in a similar position, it does the same thing.

The considerations that answer the argument of equal rights also answer the objections to treating man as a
thing, and the like. If a man lives in society, he is liable to find himself so treated. The degree of civilization that
a people has reached, no doubt, is marked by their anxiety to do as they would be done by. However, the social
instincts have not yet grown to control our actions absolutely, even in anti-social situations. As the rules of law
are based upon a morality that is generally accepted, no rule founded on a theory of absolute unselfishness can
be laid down without a breach between law and working beliefs.

If it is true that the general principles of criminal and civil liability are the same, it will follow from that alone
that theory and fact agree in frequently punishing those who have been guilty of no moral wrong, and who
could not be condemned by any standard that did not avowedly disregard the personal peculiarities of the
individuals concerned. If punishment stood on the moral grounds that are proposed for it, the first thing to be
considered would be those limitations in the capacity for choosing rightly that arise from abnormal instincts,


want of education, lack of intelligence, and all the other defects which are most marked in the criminal classes.
The criminal law is not enacted or administered on that theory.

GENERAL KNOWLEDGE

I. THREE bills moved together through Parliament in August 2025, and taken separately, each
look almost technical. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirtieth Amendment) Bill, 2025
deals with what happens to a chief minister or prime minister who is arrested. The Jammu and
Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025 and the Government of Union Territories
(Amendment) Bill, 2025 extend a similar logic to other Union Territories. But critics across the
opposition and among constitutional scholars argue that re ad together, the three bills amount to
something far larger than routine housekeeping legislation: a rewiring of how elected
governments in India can be removed from office, and by whom. At the heart of all three bills is
a single mechanism. If a prime minister, a chief minister, or a minister is arrested and held in
custody for 30 consecutive days on a charge that carries a prison term of five years or more, that
person is required to resign. If they don't, the office is deemed vacant automatically. No
conviction is required. No chargesheet needs to have been filed. No court needs to have
examined the evidence at all.


Source: https://www.dailyexcelsior.com/jpc-on-key-bills-including-jk-ut-reorganization-
amendment-defers-report-for-more-consultations/

V. Union Minister of Coal & Mines G Kishan Reddy on Friday said that the Semicon 2.0 programme, along
with the new Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS), would create significant opportunities for
Hyderabad and the youth of Telangana.
In a press statement issued here, Kishan hailed the Union Cabinet’s approval for the Semicon 2.0 programme as
a historic step towards transforming India into a global semiconductor powerhouse.


“The Centre has approved the Rs 1.27 lakh crore Semicon 2.0 programme for 12 years to strengthen India’s
semiconductor and electronics ecosystem amid global supply chain disruptions and increasing technological
competition. The Cabinet has also approved the Rs 62,500 crore MPMS, taking the total investment in the
electronics and semiconductor sector to nearly Rs 1.9 lakh crore,” he said.

Highlighting Telangana’s role in the semiconductor ecosystem, the Union minister said that under Semicon 1.0,
the Centre trained over 68,000 students across 315 universities, including those in Telangana, using advanced
Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools.
He further said that the Centre has extended Rs 724 crore funds to Electronic Manufacturing Clusters in
Telangana. “This includes Rs 252 crore for the Greenfield EMC at E-City and Fab City, Rs 139 crore for the
Maheshwaram Greenfield EMC, Rs 75 crore for a Common Facility Centre in Hyderabad and Rs 258 crore for
the EMC project at Divitipally,” he added.

Source- https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/telangana/2026/Jul/18/semicon-20-mpms-will-prove-
beneficial-for-states-youth-minister-kishan

LEGAL REASONING
I. In a significant judgment boosting the interests of transparency, the Supreme Court held that the State cannot
claim absolute immunity from the disclosure of materials by merely claiming that they are related to national
security. Quashing the decision of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to refuse renewal of the
telecast license for the Malayalam news channel MediaOne, the bench held that "concerns of national security
do not permit an absolute abrogation of the principles of natural justice".

The mere involvement of national security issues won't preclude the State's duty to act fairly: The Centre raised
the plea of "national security" to claim immunity for disclosure of the materials. Therefore, one of the issues
before the Supreme Court in the channel's appeal was whether national security was a complete exception to the
principles of natural justice. The Centre contended that decisions in Ex-Army men's Protection Services Private
Limited v. Union of India have held that the principles of natural justice have no application when national
security issues are involved.

The principle of Natural Justice is derived from the word ‘Jus Natural’ of Roman law and it is closely related to
Common law and moral principles but is not codified. The first one is audi alteram partem, i.e., “Hearing rule”
which states that the person or party who is affected by the decision made by the panel of expert members
should be given a fair opportunity to express his point of view to defend himself.
Secondly, nemo judex in causa sua, which is the “Bias rule” generally expresses that a panel of experts should
be biased-free while taking a decision. The decision should be made in a free and fair manner that can fulfil the
rule of natural justice. And thirdly, “Reasoned Decision” states that the order, decision or judgement of the court
is given by the Presiding authorities with valid and reasonable grounds.

Source: https:/Awww.livelaw.in/top-stories/national-security-concerns-principles-of-natural-justice-ib-reports-
immunity-supreme-court-mediaone-case-225589

telecast license for the Malayalam news channel MediaOne, the bench held that "concerns of national security
do not permit an absolute abrogation of the principles of natural justice".

The mere involvement of national security issues won't preclude the State's duty to act fairly: The Centre raised
the plea of "national security" to claim immunity for disclosure of the materials. Therefore, one of the issues
before the Supreme Court in the channel's appeal was whether national security was a complete exception to the
principles of natural justice. The Centre contended that decisions in Ex-Army men's Protection Services Private
Limited v. Union of India have held that the principles of natural justice have no application when national
security issues are involved.

The principle of Natural Justice is derived from the word ‘Jus Natural’ of Roman law and it is closely related to
Common law and moral principles but is not codified. The first one is audi alteram partem, i.e., “Hearing rule”
which states that the person or party who is affected by the decision made by the panel of expert members
should be given a fair opportunity to express his point of view to defend himself.
Secondly, nemo judex in causa sua, which is the “Bias rule” generally expresses that a panel of experts should
be biased-free while taking a decision. The decision should be made in a free and fair manner that can fulfil the
rule of natural justice. And thirdly, “Reasoned Decision” states that the order, decision or judgement of the court
is given by the Presiding authorities with valid and reasonable grounds.
