content.passageText:
IV. Roman wakes early. He sloughs off his sleeping bag and swims in the dark to the lab window. Where are
we, where are we? Where on earth. It's night and there’s land. Into view edges a giant city nebula among
reddish-rust-nothing; no, two cities, Johannesburg and Pretoria locked together like a binary star. Just beyond
the hoop of the atmosphere is the sun, and in the next minute it will clear the horizon and flood the earth, and
dawn will come and go in a matter of seconds before daylight is everywhere at once. Central and East Africa
suddenly bright and hot.
Today is his four hundredth and thirty-fourth day in space, a tally arrived at over three different missions. He
keeps close count. Of this mission it's day eighty-eight. In a single nine-month mission there are in total roughly
five hundred and forty hours of morning exercise. Five hundred morning and afternoon meetings with the
American, European and Russian crews on the ground. Four thousand three hundred and twenty sunrises, four
thousand three hundred and twenty sunsets. Almost one hundred and eight million miles travelled. Thirty-six
Tuesdays, for all that, this being one. Five hundred and forty times of having to swallow toothpaste. Thirty-six
changes of T-shirt, a hundred and thirty-five changes of underwear (a fresh set of underwear every day is a
storage luxury that can’t be afforded), fifty-four clean pairs of socks. Auroras, hurricanes, storms their numbers
unknown but their occurrence certain. Nine full cycles, of course, of the moon, their silver companion moving
placidly through its phases while the days go awry. But all the same the moon seen several times a day and
sometimes in strange distortion.
To his tally kept on a piece of paper in his crew quarters, Roman will add the eighty-eighth line. Not to wish the
time away but to try to tether it to something countable. Otherwise the centre drifts. Space shreds time to pieces.
They were told this in training: keep a tally each day when you wake, tell yourself this is the morning of a new
day. Be clear with yourself on this matter. This is the morning of a new day.
And so it is, but in this new day they'll circle the earth sixteen times. They'll see sixteen sunrises and sixteen
sunsets, sixteen days and sixteen nights. Roman clasps the handrail by the window to steady himself; the
southern hemisphere stars are fleeting away. You're bound to Coordinated Universal Time, ground crews tell
them. Be clear with yourself on this matter, always clear. Look often at your watch to anchor your mind, tell
yourself when you wake up: this is the morning of a new day.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions: https://lithub.com/orbital/

GENERAL KNOWLEDGE

I. Ahead of the 17th BRICS Summit, Colombia and Uzbekistan have officially joined the New Development
Bank (NDB), expanding the multilateral lender’s membership to 11 countries. Founded in 2015 by the original

II. A certificate of registration gives an organisation a recognised legal form, but its absence does not make the
organisation unlawful or invisible to the law. This distinction lies at the heart of the controversy surrounding
Karnataka Home Minister Priyank Kharge's letter to RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat. Dated June 13, 2026, the letter
sought details regarding the RSS's legal status, finances, office-bearers, assets, tax compliance, and the
permissions obtained for its public events. It also urged the organisation to register itself and requested its
authorised office-bearers to explain how it continues to function without formal registration. The controversy
stems from a common misconception that every large organisation must be registered under a corporate, trust,
society, or NGO framework. However, Indian law does not require every association of individuals to obtain
formal registration. The Constitution of India guarantees citizens the freedom to assemble peacefully and to
form associations or unions. Consequently, thousands of religious groups, spiritual congregations, cultural
organisations, community forums, and voluntary bodies across the country function lawfully without any
central registration.
Source: https://frontline.thehindu.com/politics/rss-registration-legal-debate-2026/article71136915.ece

popular with his British constituents lately, but he certainly had many friends among the European Union's top
politicians. As European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reacted to his resignation on Monday,
she wrote: "European and Ukrainian security is stronger because of you. Thank you, dear Keir." French

willing" for Ukraine, and for revitalizing EU-UK relations. It was as a supporter of Ukraine in its war against
Russia that Starmer really cemented his reputation in Europe. Together with Macron, Starmer was a leader of
the so-called "coalition of the willing." The alliance of 35 states supports Ukraine with military aid and, should
there be a ceasefire, would then help Ukraine with longer-term defense.

IV. Team of scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on May 18 shared a report of the
findings of the ‘Hop’ experiment conducted by the Vikram Lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the Chandra’s Surface
Thermophysical Experiment (ChaSTE) on the moon. The researchers noted, “While we often call it lunar soil,
the more apt term to be used is lunar regolith. The lunar regolith is actually shattered rock, tiny, jagged glass-
like shards that are abrasive and cling to everything.” They also pointed out that the complex structure of
regolith has unique geo-technical and thermophysical properties. They said the top 2-6 cm regolith is found to
be highly cohesive or sticky and hyper-porous, which can act as a thermal blanket. This layer is crucial in the
storage of water-ice molecules in the subsurface, and in selecting the sites for future scientific bases and habitat
construction on the Moon.

V. The Indian passport is a “travel document” and not a “citizenship document”, a senior official of the
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday (June 24, 2026). The purpose of the Indian passport is
to help Indians transit and travel through foreign ports and territories and it should not be compared with other
documents that are used to establish citizenship rights, the official said. A passport serves two functions: it
facilitates international travel and identifies the holder as it attests the holder’s nationality. Citizenship,
however, is a legal status defined exclusively under the Citizenship Act, 1955. The existence of a passport does
not, by itself, resolve all possible legal disputes regarding citizenship. The government’s position rests on a
technical but important distinction. A passport is evidence that the state accepted a claim of citizenship at the
time of issuance. It is not, however, a legal declaration that cannot be questioned under any circumstance.

LEGAL REASONING

I. Article 22 of the Indian Constitution outlines several rights available to an accused in the case of arrest and
detention. It mandates the duty to inform the accused of the grounds of arrest and to consult a lawyer of choice.
Additionally, it requires the police officer to present the person arrested before a magistrate within twenty-four
hours, ensuring that the individual cannot be detained beyond this period without proper judicial authority.
Under Article 22(1) and Section 41D of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), an accused person has the
right to be consulted and defended by a legal practitioner of their choice. This right is crucial, especially during
interrogation, although it does not extend throughout the entire interrogation process.
The concept of free legal aid is integral to ensuring justice for all, particularly for those who lack the economic
means to engage in legal proceedings. Article 39A of the Constitution, under the Directive Principles of State
Policy, emphasizes the state's duty to ensure justice is accessible to all citizens, thereby mandating the provision
of free legal aid. This is aimed at creating an equitable justice system where economic constraints do not hinder
access to legal recourse.
Section 54(1) of the CrPC grants the accused the right to a full-body medical examination. This examination
can be crucial in providing evidence that may either disprove the commission of an offence by the accused or
implicate someone else. However, this right is subject to the magistrate's discretion, especially if it is perceived
as a tactic to delay proceedings.
The Constitution provides a framework for the protection of individuals against arbitrary arrest and detention.
Article 22 specifically addresses these concerns, ensuring that the rights of the accused are safeguarded during
the legal process. This includes the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, the right to legal
representation, and the right to be presented before a magistrate within a specified timeframe.
An arrested individual must be informed of the reasons for their arrest. This is a fundamental right that ensures
transparency and fairness in the legal process. Additionally, the right to legal representation is critical in
safeguarding the interests of the accused, allowing them access to legal counsel to defend their case effectively.
The provisions related to arrest and detention reflect the overarching principles of justice and fairness embedded
in the Indian legal system. These provisions aim to balance the state's power to detain individuals for legal
transgressions with the fundamental rights of individuals, ensuring that the process of arrest and detention is not
abused and is conducted in a manner that respects the dignity and rights of the accused.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Arrest of Persons Under CrPC, 1973”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/arrest-of-a-person/#Protection_against_arrest_and_detention

II. In a recent Supreme Court ruling, it was determined that a Hindu couple had not legally married despite
holding a marriage certificate, as their marriage was registered under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA)
before performing the necessary wedding rituals. This decision emphasizes the requirement for fulfilling
specific ceremonial rituals to validate a marriage under the HMA, notably those outlined in Sections 7 and 5.
Section 5 of the HMA outlines the conditions for a Hindu marriage, mandating that certain conditions be met
for a marriage to be considered valid. These conditions include the requirement for neither party to have a
spouse living at the time of marriage, both parties to be of sound mind and capable of giving valid consent,
neither party suffering from mental disorders that would render them unfit for marriage and procreation, and
that the bride and groom should not fall within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.
The distinction between marriage registration and solemnization is crucial under the HMA. Solemnization
refers to the actual marriage ceremonies required by religious practices, which are essential for a marriage to be
recognized as valid under personal laws. In contrast, registration is a formal act of record-keeping that typically
follows the solemnization of the marriage. Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), a civil or "registered"
marriage occurs where the marriage is solemnized without traditional rituals in a registrar's office, and the
registration itself validates the marriage.
For Hindus and some Christian communities in India, marriage is considered a sacrament, necessitating specific
religious ceremonies for a valid union. Conversely, Islamic marriages are based on contractual principles,

requiring mutual consent and witnesses but not ceremonial rites. The nikahnama in Islamic traditions formalizes
the union and is generally recognized even without additional state registration.
Several states, including Karnataka and Delhi, mandate the registration of marriages, highlighting its
importance for legal recognition and administrative purposes. This registration is vital in contexts requiring
proof of marital status, such as applications for spousal visas or inheritance claims.
However, the non-registration of a marriage under the HMA does not inherently invalidate it if the required
rituals are observed. While a marriage certificate under the SMA is conclusive evidence of marriage, under the
HMA, the certificate alone is insufficient without the completion of specified rituals, per Sections 5 and 7.
Source: Extracted with edits and revision from https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-law/do-

Their marriage would be invalid because Sanya's condition, although occasional, could still impact her

II. In a recent Supreme Court ruling, it was determined that a Hindu couple had not legally married despite
holding a marriage certificate, as their marriage was registered under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA)
before performing the necessary wedding rituals. This decision emphasizes the requirement for fulfilling
specific ceremonial rituals to validate a marriage under the HMA, notably those outlined in Sections 7 and 5.
Section 5 of the HMA outlines the conditions for a Hindu marriage, mandating that certain conditions be met
for a marriage to be considered valid. These conditions include the requirement for neither party to have a
spouse living at the time of marriage, both parties to be of sound mind and capable of giving valid consent,
neither party suffering from mental disorders that would render them unfit for marriage and procreation, and
that the bride and groom should not fall within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.
The distinction between marriage registration and solemnization is crucial under the HMA. Solemnization
refers to the actual marriage ceremonies required by religious practices, which are essential for a marriage to be
recognized as valid under personal laws. In contrast, registration is a formal act of record-keeping that typically
follows the solemnization of the marriage. Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), a civil or "registered"
marriage occurs where the marriage is solemnized without traditional rituals in a registrar's office, and the
registration itself validates the marriage.
For Hindus and some Christian communities in India, marriage is considered a sacrament, necessitating specific
religious ceremonies for a valid union. Conversely, Islamic marriages are based on contractual principles,

requiring mutual consent and witnesses but not ceremonial rites. The nikahnama in Islamic traditions formalizes
the union and is generally recognized even without additional state registration.
Several states, including Karnataka and Delhi, mandate the registration of marriages, highlighting its
importance for legal recognition and administrative purposes. This registration is vital in contexts requiring
proof of marital status, such as applications for spousal visas or inheritance claims.
However, the non-registration of a marriage under the HMA does not inherently invalidate it if the required
rituals are observed. While a marriage certificate under the SMA is conclusive evidence of marriage, under the
HMA, the certificate alone is insufficient without the completion of specified rituals, per Sections 5 and 7.

III. The doctrine of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria" plays a critical role. This Latin maxim, translating to "no injury is
done to one who consents,” essentially states that individuals who knowingly and willingly consent to activities
bearing inherent risks are precluded from seeking damages for any resulting injury. This principle rests on the
idea that consenting adults are aware of the risks involved and, thus, cannot hold others liable if harm occurs
during such activities.
The doctrine applies primarily to cases involving clear and informed consent, where the individual understands
the nature of the risk and voluntarily agrees to accept it. Common scenarios include sports, medical procedures,
and certain contractual agreements. In each instance, the person engaged has acknowledged and accepted the
potential for harm, negating their ability to claim compensation later.
However, the application of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria” is not absolute. Legal exceptions occur when consent is
obtained through deceptive means such as fraud, coercion, or misrepresentation, rendering the consent invalid.
Moreover, the principle does not apply if the defendant's actions were illegal or if they acted with gross
negligence exceeding what was consented to.
In sports, for example, players assume the normal risks associated with the game but do not consent to conduct
that is outside the rules and could cause unexpected harm. Similarly, patients undergoing surgery give informed
consent only for the risks disclosed to them prior to the operation, not for medical negligence or errors beyond
those risks.


Furthermore, this legal doctrine is carefully evaluated in situations involving rescuers. When the plaintiff suffers
an injury as a result of him doing an act which he knows is likely to cause harm to him but it is an act to rescue
someone, then this defence will not apply and the defendant will be held liable. Therefore, they can seek redress
for injuries sustained during the rescue.
"Volenti Non Fit Injuria” also intersects with public policy, which sometimes limits its application to ensure that
individuals are not unduly pressured into accepting risks that are unreasonable or inherently dangerous.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.legalserviceindia.com/legal/article-13963-volenti-
non-fit-injuria-essentials-andexceptions.html

overwhelmed by Aman's superior technique, grabbed a wooden stick that was part of the event's

match as a result. After recovering, Aman decided to sue Rajat for damages due to the injury sustained
during the match. Rajat argues that Aman, as a professional boxer, consented to the risks inherent in
boxing. Will Aman succeed in his legal claim for damages?
options:
Yes, because Aman consented to the normal risks associated with boxing, not to being hit with a foreign
object, which is outside the rules of the sport.

No, because by participating in a professional boxing match, Aman consented to all forms of physical
contact, regardless of their nature.

No, because the use of the stick could be seen as part of the competitive strategy inherent in such a high-
stakes sports environment.

Yes, because the wooden stick caused unexpected harm, which should legally be considered within the
normal scope of the boxing match.

Late one night, Vikram, a professional swimmer, notices a car veering off a bridge into a river.
Realizing the driver is trapped inside, Vikram dives into the river despite knowing the strong currents
could be hazardous to himself. He successfully rescues the driver, but suffers a severe injury during the
rescue due to hitting submerged debris, which was not clearly visible at night. The local municipality had
been informed about the increasing debris under the bridge but had delayed cleaning it up. Vikram
decides to sue the municipality for his injuries. Will he succeed?
options:
Yes, because Vikram was injured while performing a rescue, which negates the defense that he voluntarily

III. The doctrine of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria" plays a critical role. This Latin maxim, translating to "no injury is
done to one who consents,” essentially states that individuals who knowingly and willingly consent to activities
bearing inherent risks are precluded from seeking damages for any resulting injury. This principle rests on the
idea that consenting adults are aware of the risks involved and, thus, cannot hold others liable if harm occurs
during such activities.
The doctrine applies primarily to cases involving clear and informed consent, where the individual understands
the nature of the risk and voluntarily agrees to accept it. Common scenarios include sports, medical procedures,
and certain contractual agreements. In each instance, the person engaged has acknowledged and accepted the
potential for harm, negating their ability to claim compensation later.
However, the application of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria” is not absolute. Legal exceptions occur when consent is
obtained through deceptive means such as fraud, coercion, or misrepresentation, rendering the consent invalid.
Moreover, the principle does not apply if the defendant's actions were illegal or if they acted with gross
negligence exceeding what was consented to.
In sports, for example, players assume the normal risks associated with the game but do not consent to conduct
that is outside the rules and could cause unexpected harm. Similarly, patients undergoing surgery give informed
consent only for the risks disclosed to them prior to the operation, not for medical negligence or errors beyond
those risks.


Furthermore, this legal doctrine is carefully evaluated in situations involving rescuers. When the plaintiff suffers
an injury as a result of him doing an act which he knows is likely to cause harm to him but it is an act to rescue
someone, then this defence will not apply and the defendant will be held liable. Therefore, they can seek redress
for injuries sustained during the rescue.
"Volenti Non Fit Injuria” also intersects with public policy, which sometimes limits its application to ensure that
individuals are not unduly pressured into accepting risks that are unreasonable or inherently dangerous.

non-fit-injuria-essentials-andexceptions.html

IV. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, commonly known as the anti-defection law, lays down the
circumstances in which a member of a legislature incurs disqualification on the ground of defection. A member
elected on the ticket of a political party is liable to be disqualified if the member voluntarily gives up the
membership of that political party or votes, or abstains from voting, contrary to any direction issued by the
political party without prior permission, unless such action is condoned by the political party within fifteen
days. The expression "voluntarily giving up membership" is not confined to formal resignation and may be
inferred from the conduct of the member. An independently elected member incurs disqualification upon joining
any political party after the election, while a nominated member incurs disqualification if the member joins a
political party after the expiry of six months from the date of taking a seat in the House. Any question relating to
disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or the Chairman of the House, whose
decision remains subject to judicial review.

The Constitution recognises only one exception to disqualification on the ground of defection, namely a valid
merger under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule. A member shall not be disqualified if the original political
party merges with another political party and the member acts in accordance with such merger. A member who
does not accept a valid merger is also protected from disqualification and is entitled to continue functioning as a
separate group within the House. However, constitutional protection is available only when the merger satisfies
all the conditions prescribed under Paragraph 4.
For the purposes of the Tenth Schedule, the "original political party" and the "legislature party" are distinct legal
entities. The original political party refers to the parent political organisation, whereas the legislature party
consists only of the members of that political party in a particular House. The legislature party derives its
existence and authority from the original political party and cannot function independently in matters
concerning merger. Consequently, the decision to merge must originate from the original political party. A
legislature party cannot independently initiate, declare, or create a merger with another political party, and any
such attempt does not satisfy the constitutional requirements governing mergers.

Paragraph 4(2) provides that a merger shall be deemed to have taken place only if not less than two-thirds of the
members of the legislature party concerned have agreed to such merger. The requirement of a two-thirds
majority is mandatory but is not, by itself, sufficient to constitute a valid merger. Such approval acquires legal
effect only after the original political party has resolved to merge with another political party. Therefore, a valid
merger requires the coexistence of two conditions: a merger of the original political party and the approval of
not less than two-thirds of the members of the corresponding legislature party. Failure to satisfy either condition

renders the constitutional exception inapplicable and attracts the ordinary provisions relating to disqualification
under the anti-defection law.

The constitutional position regarding mergers was strengthened by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment)
Act, 2003, which omitted the earlier provision recognising splits by one-third of the members of a legislature
party. Following the amendment, the Constitution recognises only mergers supported by not less than two-thirds
of the members of the legislature party, thereby preventing legislators from circumventing the anti-defection
law through smaller breakaway groups.
Judicial interpretation has consistently affirmed the primacy of the original political party under the Tenth
Schedule. In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that voluntary relinquishment of
party membership may be inferred from the conduct of a member and does not require a formal resignation. In
Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007), the Court rejected the "two hats theory" and held that
legislators cannot simultaneously claim an independent constitutional identity separate from the original
political party. More recently, in Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023), the
Supreme Court reaffirmed that a legislature party cannot function independently of the original political party in
matters relating to party leadership, organisational authority, or constitutional recognition. The constitutional
scheme, therefore, recognises the original political party as the primary legal entity under the Tenth Schedule,
while the legislature party functions only as its legislative manifestation. Accordingly, protection from
disqualification on the ground of merger is available only upon strict compliance with the constitutional
requirements prescribed under Paragraph 4.
Source: https://www.livelaw.in/articles/is-raghav-chaddhas-merger-with-bjp-a-valid-defence-under-
antidefection-law-531690

V. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended in 2021, regulates the conditions under which
pregnancies may be lawfully terminated in India. The Act recognises the reproductive autonomy of women


while prescribing statutory safeguards based upon the stage of pregnancy and the opinion of qualified medical
professionals. As a general rule, a pregnancy may be terminated up to twenty weeks of gestation, provided the
conditions prescribed under the Act are fulfilled and the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner is
obtained. For pregnancies between twenty and twenty-four weeks, termination is permissible only for specified
categories of women, including survivors of rape, sexual assault or incest, minors, women whose marital status
changes due to widowhood or divorce during pregnancy, women with physical disabilities recognised under the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, mentally ill women including women with mental retardation,
women carrying foetuses suffering from substantial abnormalities likely to be incompatible with life or likely to
result in serious physical or mental disability, and women whose pregnancies occur in humanitarian, disaster or
emergency situations declared by the Government. Termination during this period requires the opinion of not
less than two Registered Medical Practitioners.

The Act imposes stricter conditions once the pregnancy exceeds twenty-four weeks. Termination beyond this
stage is ordinarily prohibited and is permissible only where it is immediately necessary to save the life of the
pregnant woman or where substantial foetal abnormalities are diagnosed in accordance with the statutory
procedure. In cases involving substantial foetal abnormalities after twenty-four weeks, the opinion of the State-
level Medical Board is mandatory. The Act further permits termination of pregnancy on the ground of failure of
any contraceptive method or device, and this ground is available equally to both married and unmarried women.
Thus, while the Act recognises reproductive choice, it subjects such choice to different procedural requirements
depending upon the duration of pregnancy.

The Act also prescribes the places where pregnancy may be lawfully terminated. No termination may be carried
out except in a hospital established or maintained by the Government or at a place specifically approved for the
purposes of the Act by the Government or by a duly constituted District Level Committee. Such Committee is
required to consist of not less than three and not more than five members, with the Chief Medical Officer or
District Health Officer serving as its Chairperson. To ensure confidentiality, Section 5A prohibits a Registered
Medical Practitioner from disclosing the identity or other particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has been
terminated under the Act, except where disclosure is authorised by law. The Act also grants protection to
Registered Medical Practitioners acting in good faith by providing that no civil or criminal proceedings shall lie
against them for any act done or intended to be done in accordance with the Act.

The constitutional validity and operation of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act have repeatedly come
before constitutional courts. The Supreme Court has observed that the statutory scheme permits termination of
pregnancies beyond twenty-four weeks where substantial foetal abnormalities exist but does not ordinarily
extend similar protection to pregnancies resulting from rape or incest involving minor girls. The Court has
therefore indicated that the legislative framework may require reconsideration to remove the statutory time limit
in cases involving pregnancies of minor rape victims. The issue highlights the interaction between statutory
restrictions and constitutional guarantees of dignity, bodily autonomy and reproductive choice.

Indian constitutional jurisprudence has consistently recognised that a woman's decision whether to continue or
terminate a pregnancy forms part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the
Constitution. The constitutional protection extends to decisional autonomy, bodily integrity, privacy and the
freedom to determine whether to enter motherhood. Judicial decisions have emphasised that compelling a
woman to continue a pregnancy arising from rape may infringe her dignity and personal liberty by forcing her


to endure continuing physical and psychological trauma. Constitutional courts have therefore interpreted the
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act in a manner that seeks to balance legislative safeguards with the

V. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended in 2021, regulates the conditions under which
pregnancies may be lawfully terminated in India. The Act recognises the reproductive autonomy of women


while prescribing statutory safeguards based upon the stage of pregnancy and the opinion of qualified medical
professionals. As a general rule, a pregnancy may be terminated up to twenty weeks of gestation, provided the
conditions prescribed under the Act are fulfilled and the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner is
obtained. For pregnancies between twenty and twenty-four weeks, termination is permissible only for specified
categories of women, including survivors of rape, sexual assault or incest, minors, women whose marital status
changes due to widowhood or divorce during pregnancy, women with physical disabilities recognised under the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, mentally ill women including women with mental retardation,
women carrying foetuses suffering from substantial abnormalities likely to be incompatible with life or likely to
result in serious physical or mental disability, and women whose pregnancies occur in humanitarian, disaster or
emergency situations declared by the Government. Termination during this period requires the opinion of not
less than two Registered Medical Practitioners.

The Act imposes stricter conditions once the pregnancy exceeds twenty-four weeks. Termination beyond this
stage is ordinarily prohibited and is permissible only where it is immediately necessary to save the life of the
pregnant woman or where substantial foetal abnormalities are diagnosed in accordance with the statutory
procedure. In cases involving substantial foetal abnormalities after twenty-four weeks, the opinion of the State-
level Medical Board is mandatory. The Act further permits termination of pregnancy on the ground of failure of
any contraceptive method or device, and this ground is available equally to both married and unmarried women.
Thus, while the Act recognises reproductive choice, it subjects such choice to different procedural requirements
depending upon the duration of pregnancy.

The Act also prescribes the places where pregnancy may be lawfully terminated. No termination may be carried
out except in a hospital established or maintained by the Government or at a place specifically approved for the
purposes of the Act by the Government or by a duly constituted District Level Committee. Such Committee is
required to consist of not less than three and not more than five members, with the Chief Medical Officer or
District Health Officer serving as its Chairperson. To ensure confidentiality, Section 5A prohibits a Registered
Medical Practitioner from disclosing the identity or other particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has been
terminated under the Act, except where disclosure is authorised by law. The Act also grants protection to
Registered Medical Practitioners acting in good faith by providing that no civil or criminal proceedings shall lie
against them for any act done or intended to be done in accordance with the Act.

The constitutional validity and operation of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act have repeatedly come
before constitutional courts. The Supreme Court has observed that the statutory scheme permits termination of
pregnancies beyond twenty-four weeks where substantial foetal abnormalities exist but does not ordinarily
extend similar protection to pregnancies resulting from rape or incest involving minor girls. The Court has
therefore indicated that the legislative framework may require reconsideration to remove the statutory time limit
in cases involving pregnancies of minor rape victims. The issue highlights the interaction between statutory
restrictions and constitutional guarantees of dignity, bodily autonomy and reproductive choice.

Indian constitutional jurisprudence has consistently recognised that a woman's decision whether to continue or
terminate a pregnancy forms part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the
Constitution. The constitutional protection extends to decisional autonomy, bodily integrity, privacy and the
freedom to determine whether to enter motherhood. Judicial decisions have emphasised that compelling a
woman to continue a pregnancy arising from rape may infringe her dignity and personal liberty by forcing her


to endure continuing physical and psychological trauma. Constitutional courts have therefore interpreted the
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act in a manner that seeks to balance legislative safeguards with the
fundamental rights of women while ensuring that the statutory requirements governing gestational limits,
medical opinions, approved medical facilities and confidentiality are strictly complied with.

ofminor-rape-victim-supreme-court-to-centre-532351

opinion before 20 weeks.

VI. The Transfer of Property Act, enacted on July 1, 1882, governs property transactions in India, stipulating
clear provisions for the conditions and constituents of valid transfers. The Act primarily aims to define and
amend the law regarding property transfers by acts between parties, excluding transfers by operation of law. The
essence of a ‘transfer of property’ involves an act where one person conveys property to one or more individuals
or to himself and others. The term ‘person’ includes individuals, groups of individuals, associations, or
companies, and ‘transfer’ is broadly defined in relation to the term "convey," indicating the process of
transferring something to another party.
For a transfer to be deemed valid under the Act, several essential criteria must be met. Firstly, as per Section 5
of the Act, the transfer must occur between two or more living persons, necessitating that both the transferor and
the transferee be alive at the time of the transfer. This ensures that the property cannot be transferred to or by
deceased persons, making the act of conveyance a strictly inter vivos transaction.
Additionally, the property in question must be legally transferable. Section 6 outlines certain properties that are
inherently non-transferable, which includes exceptions such as spes successionis (the chance of an heir
succeeding), easements, right of re-entry, interests restricted to personal enjoyment, and the mere right to sue,
among others. For instance, rights that are purely personal or attached to a future maintenance cannot be
transferred. Also, stipends such as military pensions and political pensions are specified as non-transferable
under this section.
Specific instances of non-transferable property rights include the right of re-entry, which cannot be transferred
separate from the property it concerns, and stipends or pensions, which are personal to the receiver and thus
non-transferable. The prohibition against transferring a mere right to sue underscores the personal nature of
such claims, which are designed to redress personal grievances rather than transferable property rights.

Furthermore, the Act specifies that any transfer intended for unlawful purposes, or those that are inherently
fraudulent, immoral, or opposed to public policy, are void. This includes transfers for purposes that are
forbidden by law or involve or imply injury to another person or property, ensuring that property transactions
adhere to legal and ethical standards.
Section 7 of the Transfer of Property Act delineates who is competent to transfer property. To validly transfer
property, a person must be the owner or legally authorized to make the transfer. This authority may be personal,
derived from agency, or granted by law or court order. Competency requires that the person be of majority age
and sound mind, and not disqualified by any law to which they are subject.

act-1882/

clause that Sanjay also acquires the "right to sue" any third parties that Mr. Gupta is currently in
litigation with over a boundary dispute affecting the plot. Believing this to enhance the value of his
purchase, Sanjay proceeds with the deal. However, when Sanjay attempts to initiate legal proceedings
against the third parties as the new owner, he finds out that the mere "right to sue” for a personal claim
such as a boundary dispute is inherently non-transferable under the law. Sanjay decides to sue Mr. Gupta
for the invalidity of part of their agreement and demands a reduction in the purchase price or a rescission
of the contract. Can Sanjay successfully claim a reduction in the purchase price or rescind the contract
based on the invalid transfer of the "right to sue"?
options:
Yes, because the inclusion of a non-transferable right invalidates the entire agreement, allowing Sanjay to
rescind the contract.

No, because Sanjay should have known that legal rights associated with personal claims cannot be
transferred, and his lack of due diligence does not constitute grounds for contract rescission or price adjustment.

Yes, because transferring such a right is illegal, and thus the entire contract is void as it includes an illegal
term.

No, because the "right to sue" is a mere expectancy and considered inherently non-transferable under Section
6, thus not affecting the validity of the other terms of the agreement.

transferring ownership of one of his prime properties immediately to Bharti. However, the property in
question is tied to an ongoing legal dispute about the right of re-entry which Anil's competitor claims to
hold, pending a court decision. This right was established in a previous agreement signed by Anil's father,
which restricts the property's transfer until the dispute is settled. Bharti, following Anil's passing, wishes
to transfer the property to her daughter as a wedding gift. Is the property transfer legally valid?
options:

principle of promissory estoppel.
Yes, because the property was transferred to Bharti before the court's decision, making her the rightful owner.

No, because the property is subject to a right of re-entry, which is inherently non-transferable until resolved,
as per Section 6.

No, because the property is tied to spes successionis, making it non-transferable until the court confirms the
heir.

for his pioneering work in genetic engineering. The stipend is specifically awarded to support his research
and personal expenses while he completes his groundbreaking project. Due to financial difficulties, Dr.
Aarav decides to assign half of his future stipend payments to his colleague, Dr. Priya, in exchange for an
immediate lump sum payment to cover his urgent expenses. Dr. Priya agrees, hoping the stipend support
will help further her own research in a related field. However, upon reviewing the agreement, the

VI. The Transfer of Property Act, enacted on July 1, 1882, governs property transactions in India, stipulating
clear provisions for the conditions and constituents of valid transfers. The Act primarily aims to define and
amend the law regarding property transfers by acts between parties, excluding transfers by operation of law. The
essence of a ‘transfer of property’ involves an act where one person conveys property to one or more individuals
or to himself and others. The term ‘person’ includes individuals, groups of individuals, associations, or
companies, and ‘transfer’ is broadly defined in relation to the term "convey," indicating the process of
transferring something to another party.
For a transfer to be deemed valid under the Act, several essential criteria must be met. Firstly, as per Section 5
of the Act, the transfer must occur between two or more living persons, necessitating that both the transferor and
the transferee be alive at the time of the transfer. This ensures that the property cannot be transferred to or by
deceased persons, making the act of conveyance a strictly inter vivos transaction.
Additionally, the property in question must be legally transferable. Section 6 outlines certain properties that are
inherently non-transferable, which includes exceptions such as spes successionis (the chance of an heir
succeeding), easements, right of re-entry, interests restricted to personal enjoyment, and the mere right to sue,
among others. For instance, rights that are purely personal or attached to a future maintenance cannot be
transferred. Also, stipends such as military pensions and political pensions are specified as non-transferable
under this section.
Specific instances of non-transferable property rights include the right of re-entry, which cannot be transferred
separate from the property it concerns, and stipends or pensions, which are personal to the receiver and thus
non-transferable. The prohibition against transferring a mere right to sue underscores the personal nature of
such claims, which are designed to redress personal grievances rather than transferable property rights.

Furthermore, the Act specifies that any transfer intended for unlawful purposes, or those that are inherently
fraudulent, immoral, or opposed to public policy, are void. This includes transfers for purposes that are
forbidden by law or involve or imply injury to another person or property, ensuring that property transactions
adhere to legal and ethical standards.
Section 7 of the Transfer of Property Act delineates who is competent to transfer property. To validly transfer
property, a person must be the owner or legally authorized to make the transfer. This authority may be personal,
derived from agency, or granted by law or court order. Competency requires that the person be of majority age
and sound mind, and not disqualified by any law to which they are subject.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/necessities-transfer-transfer-property-
act-1882/

anti-dumping duty was imposed on the recommendation of the Commerce Ministry and will be applicable on
tiles with at least lamination on one side. These boards are largely used for the construction industry for ceilings
in both commercial and residential projects.
Last week, the Finance Ministry imposed a definitive anti-dumping duty on certain Chinese industrial laser
machines used for cutting, marking, or welding. This move is part of a broader strategy to protect domestic
industries from unfair competition and dumping practices.
Anti-dumping duties are a form of trade protectionism imposed by a domestic government to shield local
industries from foreign competition. They are typically levied when a foreign company sells goods in a
domestic market at a price lower than their normal value, often defined as the price at which they are sold in
their home market or at a price below the cost of production. The rationale behind anti-dumping measures is to
ensure fair trade practices and prevent foreign companies from dumping their products at artificially low prices,
which can harm the local industry.
The imposition of anti-dumping duties on gypsum boards and tiles from China is a significant step by the Indian
government to protect its domestic construction industry. Gypsum boards are a critical component in the
construction sector, used extensively for ceilings and interior walls in both residential and commercial
buildings. The decision to impose duties on these imports is likely to have a considerable impact on the market
dynamics, potentially leading to changes in supply chains and pricing structures.
The move to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese industrial laser machines is also notable. These machines
are used in various industrial applications, including cutting, marking, and welding. The imposition of duties on
these products indicates the government's intent to safeguard the domestic manufacturing sector from unfair
pricing practices by foreign competitors.
Overall, these measures reflect the Indian government's commitment to protecting its industries and ensuring a
level playing field for domestic companies. By imposing anti-dumping duties, the government aims to prevent
the adverse effects of dumping on the local economy and support the growth and sustainability of Indian
industries.

III. India has imposed a definitive anti-dumping duty on gypsum board and tiles from China for five years. The
anti-dumping duty was imposed on the recommendation of the Commerce Ministry and will be applicable on
tiles with at least lamination on one side. These boards are largely used for the construction industry for ceilings
in both commercial and residential projects.
Last week, the Finance Ministry imposed a definitive anti-dumping duty on certain Chinese industrial laser
machines used for cutting, marking, or welding. This move is part of a broader strategy to protect domestic
industries from unfair competition and dumping practices.
Anti-dumping duties are a form of trade protectionism imposed by a domestic government to shield local
industries from foreign competition. They are typically levied when a foreign company sells goods in a
domestic market at a price lower than their normal value, often defined as the price at which they are sold in
their home market or at a price below the cost of production. The rationale behind anti-dumping measures is to
ensure fair trade practices and prevent foreign companies from dumping their products at artificially low prices,
which can harm the local industry.
The imposition of anti-dumping duties on gypsum boards and tiles from China is a significant step by the Indian
government to protect its domestic construction industry. Gypsum boards are a critical component in the
construction sector, used extensively for ceilings and interior walls in both residential and commercial
buildings. The decision to impose duties on these imports is likely to have a considerable impact on the market
dynamics, potentially leading to changes in supply chains and pricing structures.
The move to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese industrial laser machines is also notable. These machines
are used in various industrial applications, including cutting, marking, and welding. The imposition of duties on
these products indicates the government's intent to safeguard the domestic manufacturing sector from unfair
pricing practices by foreign competitors.
Overall, these measures reflect the Indian government's commitment to protecting its industries and ensuring a
level playing field for domestic companies. By imposing anti-dumping duties, the government aims to prevent
the adverse effects of dumping on the local economy and support the growth and sustainability of Indian
industries.


Source: https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/economy/foreign-trade/centre-imposes-anti-dumping-duty-
on-gypsum-board-from-china/articleshow/106308589.cms

IV. Though every leader has a vision, they realise that “has” is not a static term. Maybe “lives with” is more
accurate, since any starter-vision can evolve. It's subject to experience. So, of course, a leader must evolve along
with their vision. How else can they accommodate it? Over time, there's a give and take. Pursuing a vision is an
organic process where you're also redesigning yourself. Does this sound a little New Age? It's not. Just think
about it.
Any vision that we see for ourselves as it slowly, even painfully comes into focus must sync up with how we
work on ourselves to achieve it. Along the way, we can’t expect total clarity as to who we may become. We may
even ask fundamental questions about whether we are up to the task and, even more fundamentally, whether
what we are trying to achieve is right for us.
In other words, questions will arise as to who we are and who we want to be, which only we can answer. No one
else can do our introspection for us. No one else has our imagination. So, my point is that setting out to make a
vision a reality requires that we understand what motivates us, what really makes us tick.
At the very least, in becoming a leader we should be confident that that's what we really want. It's one thing to
have an abstract idea and another to integrate that idea with our lives. Are we willing to sacrifice, and
experience the demands on our time that are required if we commit to such an effort? Can we put up with the
displacement of what used to be our priorities? Can we brush off comments by people who sigh, “I don’t know
you anymore you’re so obsessed”? In effect, when we start living our vision, we must be able to live with
ourselves (though we may not have anticipated the challenges that that might entail).
Of course, we project our vision outwards, onto the world. But living with a vision draws us back towards
ourselves in an exercise of getting to know who we are and feeling comfortable with that. If we're not
comfortable with ourselves, then it will be hard to maintain a vision, much less work towards making it a
reality. If you display some misgivings towards yourself, it's unlikely that other people will be willing to follow
your lead. They may wonder, for example, “If that person is so uncomfortable with what they think, why should
I be any less so?” If you pick up on their hesitancy, you may become even less sure of yourself, creating a
vision-killer vicious circle.
Source: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/resilience/202312/as-your-vision-of-leadership-evolves-so-
does-your-life

I. "The quality of mercy" is a speech given by Portia in William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (Act 4, Scene 1).
In the speech, Portia, disguised as a lawyer, begs Shylock to show mercy to Antonio. The speech extols the power of
mercy, "an attribute to God Himself."
The quality of mercy is not strain'd.
It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest:
It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes
The thronéd monarch better than his crown.
His scepter shows the force of temporal power,
The attribute to awe and majesty
Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings;
But mercy is above this sceptered sway.
It is enthroned in the hearts of kings;
It is an attribute to God Himself;
And earthly power doth then show likest God's
When mercy seasons justice. Therefore, Jew,
Though justice be thy plea, consider this:
That in the course of justice none of us
Should see salvation. We do pray for mercy,
And that same prayer doth teach us all to render
The deeds of mercy. I have spoke thus much
To mitigate the justice of thy plea,
Which, if thou follow, this strict court of Venice
Must needs give sentence 'gainst the merchant there.
Source: Portia, in William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, Scene 1.

options: A mighty river.

II. The Gujarat High Court recently mandated the expedited installation of CCTV cameras in the Registry in a strategic
manner to prevent any tampering with court documents. This decision came after an incident where it was discovered that
someone had intentionally interfered with the listing of a case on the ‘admission board’ of a judge. The judge observed
that this was a clear attempt to obstruct the administration of justice and emphasized that such activities, especially in the
Registry of the state's highest court, cannot be tolerated. The court highlighted the lack of comprehensive CCTV coverage
in the Registry, which hindered the collection of conclusive evidence in this particular case.
The incident in question involved a practicing advocate, who, along with others in his circle, was known for engaging in
such practices, particularly in the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT). The advocate had filed a petition in 2020 to quash a
case against him, where he was initially booked for demanding a bribe while acting as a court-appointed commissioner for
the DRT Ahmedabad.
The judge had previously indicated reluctance to consider the advocate's plea and had directed the Bar Council of Gujarat
to initiate proceedings against the lawyer for professional misconduct. The case was listed on the ‘admission board’ but
was later found to have been tampered with and posted as item number 200 in the ‘final hearing board,’ a tactic to avoid a
hearing since the court typically hears cases up to item number 70 in the daily list.
In 2016, the then Chief Justice of the High Court had approved the installation of CCTVs in all judicial departments of the
Registry to ensure the safety of judicial proceedings. However, despite specific approval and the urgency of the matter,
there had been no progress in installing the cameras. The court expressed concern over this delay and ordered the
Registrar General, along with the Registrar (Vigilance) and (Judicial), to coordinate with the additional secretary of the
Chief Justice to expedite the process of installing CCTVs in every corner of the Registry and, if necessary, in the
courtrooms as well. This task was directed to be completed by January 15, 2024.
The court's decision underscores the importance of transparency and security in judicial proceedings and the need for
effective measures to prevent any interference with the administration of justice.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions: https://www.barandbench.com/news/gujarat-highcourt-orders-installation-
cctvs-registry-courtrooms-tampering-case-listing

To implement a broad strategy aimed at preventing any future interference with judicial proceedings.
To enhance the overall surveillance of legal processes, focusing on daily activities within the judiciary.
To respond to a singular incident of misconduct, ensuring such specific cases are closely monitored.

III. At some point in life, we all experience the sting of loneliness. During such times, we often feel unsupported and
become despondent, succumbing to worry and anxiety. Life's pendulum swings between moments of joy and times of
sorrow, and in the midst of turmoil, we may find ourselves anxious, fearful, and even angry. Caught in a downward spiral,
it becomes challenging to break free from the web of negativity and pessimism we weave for ourselves.
In these moments of helplessness, we seek an anchor to weather life's storms. Saints and mystics suggest a way out,
advising that when our boat is caught in a storm, we should avoid creating another storm by adding to the turmoil. The
key to navigating through the storm is to remain calm and still, anchoring ourselves in God.
The scriptures of various faiths remind us that the divine is always with us, offering support. However, we often feel
lonely because we are accustomed to living at the level of our physical senses. Our physical eyes and ears are limited to
perceiving only a certain range of matter and frequencies. Despite this, God is always beside us, guiding us through life's


difficulties. To experience God, we must transcend the physical senses, which is where the practice of meditation comes
in. A spiritual Master can teach us to still the mind, transcend physical senses, and focus our attention on the inner
spiritual world, revealing a realm of joy, peace, tranquility, and bliss.
God, being all consciousness and spirit, cannot be experienced through physical senses. To truly experience the divine, we
must follow the path laid out by saints and spiritual Masters. They found God in silence. By withdrawing from the outer
world's chatter, sitting in silence, and stilling the body and mind, we can transcend physical body consciousness and
embark on an inner journey. This journey allows us to commune with God and experience His presence firsthand. The
more we sit in silence and focus within, the closer we get to God, fulfilling life’s purpose of merging our soul back into
the Creator.
As we experience God's presence, we anchor ourselves in the stability of His love. Life's challenges no longer overwhelm
us; instead, we ride the wave, knowing that 'this too shall pass.’ The pangs of loneliness dissipate when we realize that we
are never truly alone. Regular meditation and connection with the inner Light help us recognize His presence in our lives.
God's love, ever-present, carries us through life's ups and downs, providing strength to face any circumstance with hope
and positivity.

IV. A recent scientific observation revealed that Mars' atmosphere underwent a significant expansion due to an unusual
solar wind event. This incident was recorded when a spacecraft in orbit around Mars detected a stark change in the
Martian atmosphere on a specific date in December 2022. The expansion of Mars' magnetosphere and ionosphere was so
extensive that it resulted in a tripling of its size. This dramatic change was caused by a void created by an intense gust of
solar wind.
This type of phenomenon is not entirely unprecedented. A similar incident occurred in the late 1990s when Earth's
magnetosphere experienced a substantial outward swelling, caused by a sudden decrease in solar wind, leading to a
dramatic increase in its volume. These occurrences provide a rare glimpse into the dynamics of planetary interactions with
their surrounding environments in the solar system, especially under varying solar conditions.
The study's lead researcher expressed initial scepticism upon witnessing the drastic reduction in solar wind and the
consequent atmospheric changes. The research has shed light on Mars’ response to unusual solar system conditions,
offering valuable insights.
Solar wind, a continuous flow of particles from the Sun, exerts a consistent pressure throughout the solar system,
diminishing at a boundary known as the heliopause. The event on Mars, however, involved an atypical scenario where two
solar winds interacted: a slower wind was overtaken by a faster one, resulting in a combined, more powerful 'superwind.'
The spacecraft recorded an increased particle density in this merged solar wind. Subsequently, a notable decrease in
particle density was observed, indicating an uncommonly low-density and weak solar wind.

I. Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman has been elected president of the 81st session of the United Nations
General Assembly after defeating Cyprus’s Ambassador Andreas Kakouris in a closely contested vote, taking the helm of
the world’s most representative diplomatic body at a time of mounting pressure on the multilateral system. In the secret
ballot held on Tuesday, Rahman secured 99 votes, eight more compared with his competitor Kakouris. A total of 190
ballots were cast, with no invalid votes or abstentions. The presidency rotates among the UN’s five regional groups, and
the 81st session falls to the Asia Pacific group. His presidency will coincide with one of the most consequential processes
on the UN calendar: the selection of Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’s successor, whose term expires at the end of
this year. Rahman served as national security adviser and high representative on the Rohingya issue before becoming
Bangladesh’s foreign minister in February when the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won in the country’s first
election since a student-led uprising ousted longtime leader Sheikh Hasina in 2024. A career diplomat, he joined
Bangladesh’s foreign service in 1979. He also held senior UN positions in New York and Geneva, according to UN News.
“The UN will commence its ninth decade at a time when trust in our organisation is being tested on multiple fronts,” he
told diplomats assembled at the UNGA as he accepted the new role. “Taken together, these challenges tend to undermine


the public trust and confidence in the ability of our organisation to deliver its promises.”

content.passageText:
II. In the skies over Rajasthan on June 27, 2026, an IndiGo Airbus A320 lined up for Udaipur and let satellites bring it
down. Most runways guide a jet in with a radio beam fired from the ground. Udaipur did not need to. The aircraft already
knew exactly where it was, because a system called Gagan was watching from orbit and correcting its position in real
time.
While the Indian Space Research Organisation aced the Gagan integration, its other space navigation system is in trouble.
NavIC, the country's homegrown answer to GPS, has quietly slipped below the minimum strength it needs to work at all.
Two Indian navigation systems. One is landing jets, the other fighting to stay alive. But India needs both functioning at
their optimal capacity. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) said that while similar satellite-based
approaches had earlier been carried out on smaller turboprop aircraft, this was the first such landing involving a
commercial narrow-body passenger jet using the system.
The flight performed a Localiser Performance with Vertical Guidance (LPV) approach, which provides both horizontal
and vertical guidance to pilots during landing. Such operations using Gagan had so far been limited to turboprop aircraft.


Gagan stands for GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation and is a satellite-based augmentation system that enhances the
accuracy of GPS signals. It does not work as a standalone navigation system but corrects GPS errors using data from
ground stations and satellites.
Source- https://www.outlookbusiness.com/industry/indigo-a320-makes-history-becomes-first-passenger-jet-to-land-
using-gagan-system-in-india

III. Embarking on its commitments towards positive climate actions, India has been periodically raising its ambition
towards mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and after the update in 2022, has now announced its targets for 2031-35
marking a significant step towards the goal of achieving net-zero by 2070. India’s original climate commitments i.e NDC
submitted in 2015, laid a strong foundation, with targets by 2030 of 33–35% reduction in the emissions intensity of GDP
and 40% share of non-fossil resources based electric power installed capacity, both of which were met, 11 years and 9
years ahead of the committed timelines, demonstrating a credible and action-oriented approach to climate governance.
Our emissions intensity has since reduced by 36% during 2005 to 2020, and the target has now been enhanced to 47% to
be achieved by 2035. Towards the updated NDC’s goal on enhancing share of non-fossil fuel energy resources in installed
electric power capacity, the country has achieved 52.57 % non-fossil capacity (February 2026), successfully meeting the
target five years ahead of the timeline and now the ambition has been further raised to 60% share of non-fossil fuel-based
energy resources in installed electric power capacity to be achieved by 2035. Further on the NDC goal of creating
additional carbon sink through forest and tree cover, India has already created 2.29 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by
2021 Afforestation and ecosystem restoration efforts continue to contribute towards India’s carbon sink targets while
supporting rural livelihoods. Our afforestation efforts have been duly acknowledged by independent agencies such as
Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) which has ranked India as third in terms of net gain in forest area and ninth in
terms of area under forest. This progress is a testimony to the fact that India has maintained a balance between economy
and ecology even as it maintains a high GDP growth rate. Now, we have further enhanced the ambition of creating carbon
sink through forest and tree cover to 3.5-4.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2035 from 2005 level.

Source- https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/op-ed/a-unified-policy-architecture-for-indias-energy-

IV. India and Japan have announced their first-ever defence co-development project, the Naval Radio Antenna
'UNICORN' (Unified Complex Radio Antenna with Prime Minister Narendra Modi describing it as a "new chapter" in the
defence technology partnership between the two nations.Speaking alongside Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in
New Delhi, PM Modi said the project would "open a new chapter" and that the two countries would "jointly develop
defence technologies that strengthen regional peace, maritime security, and the rules-based order."

The original agreement was signed in Tokyo way back in November 2024. It was signed by India’s Ambassador to Japan,
Sibi George, and Ishikawa Takeshi of Japan’s technology agency, ATLA. This deal was officially confirmed during the
16th India-Japan Annual Summit in New Delhi, where Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was also present. With
this, India has become the second Asian country, after the Philippines, to receive this advanced Japanese technology.

UNICORN solves this problem beautifully. By hiding all the antennas inside one smooth dome, it greatly reduces the
signals that bounce back. As a result, UNICORN can reduce the Radar Cross Section by a substantial margin, some
estimates say close to half, compared to older masts. In simple words, the warship almost becomes a ghost on enemy
radar, much harder to spot and much safer during battle.

Source- https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/defence/news/japans-ninja-tech-to-give-indias-warships-greater-
stealth-all-about-the-unicorn-masts/articleshow/132139497.cms

economies. Despite this progress, India continues to be behind four South Asian neighbours Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal
and Sri Lanka, in the global rankings.

LEGAL REASONING

I. In a significant judgment, the Supreme Court of India has clarified the legal position regarding the transfer of title of
immovable property. The Court emphasized that the transfer of title cannot be achieved through sale agreements or
general power of attorney (GPA) alone. This decision reinforces the importance of statutory provisions in the transfer of
immovable property, particularly those outlined in the Registration Act, 1908, and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, play a crucial role in this context. Section 17 mandates the compulsory
registration of certain documents related to immovable property. It specifies the types of documents that require
compulsory registration, ensuring legal sanctity and public record of transactions. Section 49 further strengthens this
requirement by stating that documents requiring compulsory registration, if unregistered, will not affect any immovable
property nor confer any power to adopt. Additionally, such unregistered documents cannot be received as evidence of any
transaction affecting such property. This provision safeguards against fraudulent transactions and ensures clarity in
property titles. Moreover, Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, is pivotal in understanding the legal
framework for the sale of immovable property. This section stipulates that a sale of immovable property can only be made
through a registered instrument. It clarifies that a mere agreement to sell, without proper registration, does not create any
interest or charge on such property. This legal provision is fundamental in ensuring that the transfer of property rights is
not merely based on informal agreements but is backed by a legally recognized and registered document.
The Supreme Court's decision is in line with its earlier judgments, which have consistently held that title in immovable
property can only be transferred through a registered deed. This position is not just a procedural formality but a legal
necessity to maintain clear property titles and avoid disputes. The judgment reiterates that transactions like sale
agreements or GPAs, while they may have some legal recognition, cannot by themselves result in the transfer of title if
they are not accompanied by duly registered conveyance deeds.
This ruling has far-reaching implications, particularly in real estate transactions. It underscores the need for due diligence
and adherence to statutory requirements in property dealings. The judgment serves as a reminder that while sale
agreements and GPAs are common in property transactions, they must be complemented by proper registration to
effectuate a legal transfer of title.

Agreement Or General Power Of Attorney: Supreme Court”, https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/no-transfer-of-title-of-

II. The law of torts is a collection of all the circumstances in which court gives a remedy by way of damages, for legally
unjustified harm or injury done by one to another person. There are three elements which need to be proved before
constituting a tort:
    There must be an act or omission on the part of the defendant.
    That act or omission should be in violation of a legal right vested in the plaintiff.
    The wrongful act or omission thus done by the defendant is of such a nature to give rise to a legal remedy.
Damnum sine Injuria refers to damages without injury or damages where no legal right of the plaintiff is infringed. The
principle is that if one exercises his rights, without infringing another’s legal right, it doesn't give rise to an action in tort.
An example cited is the case of Mayor & Co. of Bradford vs. Pickles (1895), where the defendant's act of digging a well
cut the water supply to the corporations well. The court ruled in favour of the defendant as no legal right was violated.
In the case of Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd vs. McGregor, Gow & Co. is cited, the plaintiff, an independent ship-owner,
suffered losses due to the actions of defendant ship-owners. The court ruled that the defendants acted within the law, even
if it caused harm to the plaintiff.
Injuria sine damno is a violation of a legal right without causing harm or damage. Whenever a legal right is infringed, the
person in whom the right is vested can take action. An example is Ashby Vs. White (1703), where the plaintiff, a voter, was
wrongfully denied his vote by the defendant, a returning officer. Even though the candidate he wished to vote for won, the
defendants were held liable for infringing on the plaintiff's legal right.
In the case of Bhim Singh vs. State of Jammu & Kashmir, Bhim Singh, an MLA, was arrested and prevented from
attending a legislative assembly session. The court ruled in his favor, stating a violation of his rights under Articles 21 &
22 of the Constitution.
Damnum Sine Injuria pertains to moral wrongs without legal remedies, while Injuria Sine Damnum concerns legal wrongs
that are actionable even without actual loss. The former emphasizes actions within legal bounds that may cause harm,
while the latter focuses on the violation of legal rights.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “Damnum Sine injuria & Injuria Sine Damnum: All you must know”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/damnum-injuria/

unjustified harm or injury done by one to another person. There are three elements which need to be proved before
constituting a tort:

principle is that if one exercises his rights, without infringing another’s legal right, it doesn't give rise to an action in tort.
An example cited is the case of Mayor & Co. of Bradford vs. Pickles (1895), where the defendant's act of digging a well
cut the water supply to the corporations well. The court ruled in favour of the defendant as no legal right was violated.

suffered losses due to the actions of defendant ship-owners. The court ruled that the defendants acted within the law, even
if it caused harm to the plaintiff.

person in whom the right is vested can take action. An example is Ashby Vs. White (1703), where the plaintiff, a voter, was
wrongfully denied his vote by the defendant, a returning officer. Even though the candidate he wished to vote for won, the
defendants were held liable for infringing on the plaintiff's legal right.

attending a legislative assembly session. The court ruled in his favor, stating a violation of his rights under Articles 21 &
22 of the Constitution.

III. A contract is deemed complete when there is an offer and its acceptance, along with the fulfillment of other basic
requirements such as free consent, lawful consideration, and competency. However, a contract can terminate before
finality between the promisor and promisee if certain stipulations are fulfilled, known as revocation.


Revocation is the act of annulment. Section 5 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, stipulates that a contract can be revoked
any time before the communication of acceptance is made to the proposer. Once acceptance is communicated, the contract
cannot be revoked. Section 6 lays down the methods by which a revocation of a proposal can be made, and this article
elaborates on these methodologies prescribed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
One method is the revocation of a proposal by communication of notice, where a proposal may be revoked by the
proposer by giving notice to the offeree before it is accepted. Another method is revocation by lapse of time. If there is a
time period prescribed for acceptance, the proposal gets revoked if the acceptance is not communicated before the expiry
of the prescribed time period.
A proposal can also be revoked if the condition precedent to acceptance is not fulfilled. If the offeree fails to comply with
certain conditions before acceptance of the proposal, the proposal can revoke the offer. Death or insanity of the proposer is
another method by which a proposal can be revoked, if the fact of his death or insanity comes into the knowledge of the
offeree before the communication of acceptance.
Other methods include rejection of the proposal, death of the offeree, making a counter offer, acceptance not being made
in the mode prescribed, subsequent illegality or destruction of the subject matter of a proposal. For instance, a proposal is
revoked if a counter offer is made to it, and the acceptance of the counter offer amounts to rejection of the original offer.
Contracts are considered closed when the acceptance is communicated, and revocation has an overriding effect over the
accepted principles of communication of proposal and acceptance of proposal. The courts sometimes interfere in such
cases by modifying the contract between the parties, but it is not their duty to make the contracts for the parties. The
interpretation of law involved often leads to courts being asked to examine the validity of the revocation of a proposal,
emphasizing that revocation is a statutorily provided right of both parties.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from “How revocation of proposal is made”,
https://blog.ipleaders.in/revocation-proposal-made/

IV. While holding that irretrievable breakdown of a marriage can be a ground to grant a divorce by invoking powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court clarified that a party cannot file a writ petition under Article 32
of the Constitution of India and seek relief of dissolution of marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of
marriage directly from it.
The Constitution Bench approved the view taken in the judgment Poonam v. Sumit Tanwar (2010) that the parties should
not be permitted to file a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, or for that matter under Article 226 of
the Constitution of India before the High Court, and seek divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
The Writ of Habeas Corpus is issued by the Courts in those cases where a person is illegally detained. Habeas Corpus
means ‘to have the body’ and it is one of the most effective remedies available to a person detained. The Court commands
the person or authority who has detained or restrained another person to present such person before the Court. The Court
requires the detaining person to provide the grounds on which the person has been detained and if he fails to provide a
valid ground, the person who has been detained will be released by the Court immediately.
Certiorari is a Writ that can be issued when the superior court wants to decide a matter in the case itself or if there is an
excess of jurisdiction by the inferior court. This Writ can also be issued when there is a fundamental error in the procedure
followed, or in cases of violation of the principles of natural justice.
The Writ of Quo Warranto is issued by the courts against a private person when he assumes an office on which he has no
right. Quo Warranto means ‘by what authority’ and it is an effective measure to prevent people from taking over public

offices. Writ of Prohibition is not issued often and is an extraordinary remedy that a Superior Court issues to an inferior
court or tribunal for stopping them from deciding a case because these courts do not have the jurisdiction. If the court or
tribunal does not have jurisdiction and it still decides the case, it will be an invalid judgement because for an act to be
legal it should have the sanction of law.

breakdown-227646
